About Camille Farrah Lenain

Camille Farrah Lenain (b. 1990) is a French‑Algerian photographer and educator based between New Orleans and New York. Exploring identity, memory, and belonging, her work challenges social preconception by centering communities and experiences that resist simplistic narratives. Her practice combines immersive research, portraiture, and sound, creating work that amplifies voices often overlooked or misunderstood.

She studied photography at l’ESA in Brussels and the International Center of Photography in New York. Her photographs have been exhibited at institutions and festivals worldwide including the Arab World Institute, Ogden Museum of Southern Art and Photoville. In 2024, she was recognized with the Arnold Newman Prize for New Directions in Photographic Portraiture, the U.S. Leica Women Foto Prize, and the Aperture Creators Lab. She teaches photography at Tulane University and has held residencies at the Joan Mitchell Center and the Center of Photography at Woodstock.

Foreword

Beginning as a personal act of remembrance and love letter to her uncle, Farid, Made of Smokeless Fire evolved into a collective portrait of queer Muslim life in France. Rather than seeking to explain or define its subjects, Camille Farrah Lenain’s photographs navigate the fragile space between visibility and anonymity, asking how portraiture might represent lives that are so often assumed not to exist. Shaped by years of conversation, trust and collaboration, the work rejects singular narratives in favour of emotional complexity, exploring faith identity and belonging through images that resist easy interpretation. In conversation with Nathan Leigh Taylor, Lenain reflects on transforming personal grief into a collaborative practice, photographing ‘the invisible’, the responsibility of carrying other peoples’ stories, and why Made of Smokeless Fire became, above all, an emotional landscape rather than a documentary record.

Interview

Made of Smokeless Fire began as an act of remembrance, and you’ve described the project as a love letter to your uncle, Farid. Could you tell me a little more about your relationship with him and how it shaped the work?

My family is French-Algerian. They immigrated to France in the 1950s, and I come from a large family – my grandparents had nine children. Part of the family lived in Paris: my mother, my uncle and my aunts. I grew up mostly in Paris, so they were the people I spent weekends, birthdays and family dinners with. They still are. My uncle was a central part of that group. As far as I can remember, I always knew my uncle was gay. I don’t remember there ever being a sit-down conversation explaining it. It was just how things were. He also had AIDS and diabetes, so he was ill a lot of the time. I remember years of conversations with my mum where we didn’t know whether it would be the last time we’d see him. That uncertainty was just part of life.

He passed away in 2013, and that was a really difficult time for our family. I’d already lost two other uncles before he died, but his death was particularly hard because he was one of the youngest of my grandparents’ nine children. He was the glue that held our family together. He was always laughing, making jokes, teasing everyone. He was everybody’s favourite. I think you’re allowed to say that once someone has passed away. Only a few years later, I started feeling this need to speak with him about questions of sexuality, attraction and desire. He was the only figure in my family I felt I could have asked those questions. Having those conversations with a family member is something very particular. There’s a form of acceptance that comes simply from seeing yourself represented within your blood family. It’s different from finding other queer people elsewhere.

Because he was ill with AIDS during the 1990s, his diagnosis almost became a form of coming out. Of course, not everyone with AIDS was gay, but at that time it often meant families were confronted with conversations they hadn’t had before. I wanted to understand what his life had been like as an Arab man in France, and what the gay community in Paris had been like for him. I was curious about his relationship with God and how he reconciled faith and homosexuality.

When I tried speaking about all of this with my mother and my aunts, I didn’t really get any answers. I don’t think they were ready to talk about it as the grief was still too heavy. Eventually, I reached out to a gay French-Algerian Imam living in Marseille who was HIV positive that I’d heard about. He invited me to spend time with him and a group of queer Muslim people in Marseille during one of their retreats. That was really where Made of Smokeless Fire began.

From those first conversations in Marseille, how did the project evolve beyond your uncle’s story into a collective portrait of queer Muslim life in France?

I think it really happened during that weekend and over the course of that summer. It was a big entrance into this world. I spent four days with a group of around ten or fifteen people, taking part in different activities, having conversations and showing photographs of my uncle while telling his story.

At first, I was really trying to relate everything back to him. People would look at his photographs and say, “He reminds me of my brother,” or “I feel like I know him.” In that sense, he became the glue that brought all these people together. He’s always remained central to the project and to those conversations. Everyone I’ve photographed has either seen a photograph of my uncle or heard me speak about him.

Part of this work is about challenging the stigma and stereotypes surrounding queer Muslim lives. People are often told that they cannot exist. There’s this widespread assumption that, if you’re queer, you’ll inevitably be rejected by your religion, your family and your community – that Islam is somehow the worst religion in which to be queer. I don’t think that’s entirely true. They’re all complicated. Every religion has its own tensions and contradictions.

What began as a way of understanding my uncle’s story gradually became about understanding a much larger issue that so many people were navigating. After a year or two, I also became much more interested in religion itself. At the beginning, I was really thinking through Muslim culture because it related to my own family and Arabic experience. Later, I became increasingly interested in the broader relationship between queerness and faith, and that expanded the project even further.

I think, ultimately, it was about understanding that there isn’t a single story. I became deeply committed to listening to the nuances of each person’s experience. There are threads that connect everyone, but together they form a much larger web.

This retreat in Marseille. Could you tell me a bit more about that?

Yes. It was organised by an institute called CALEM and Ludovic-Mohamed Zahed, the Imam I mentioned earlier. It brought together people from all over France, and even beyond. For example, there was someone there who had travelled from Canada and was originally from Pakistan. The retreat was also connected with other Marseille-based organisations, including an organisation that supports LGBTQ+ migrants. People from those organisations would come along as well.

Over the course of the retreat, we shared meals together, prayed together and took part in different activities. We held discussions and had social gatherings. We’d also spend time together around the city, going out dancing and enjoying being together.

Was it specifically for LGBTQ+ Muslim people, or was it open to people from all walks of life?

It was specifically for LGBTQ+ Muslim people and their allies. There was also a gay priest there, for example, who was openly welcoming of queer Muslims, and he shared his own experiences and perspective from a Christian point of view.

That’s fantastic.

It really was amazing.

I’ve been reading a bit about Ludovic-Mohamed Zahed – you mentioned him just now. With those early encounters, did he shape the work? Did those meetings really get the project moving?

Yes, definitely. Through his research and through the people I met at that retreat, the project really began to take shape. Ludovic-Mohamed is very much a scholar, but my background is not academic so I was not comfortable, nor interested in, approaching it this way. What was important for me was the community that gathered around him, because it allowed me to meet so many different people. He was certainly influential in the beginning, but I also didn’t want the project to remain entirely within his circle or be framed solely through his research. I wanted to carry out my own outreach as well.

That same year I went to Radical Pride in Paris. Six years ago, it looked very different from today. There was very little visible representation of queer Muslims and Arabs, although I think that’s changed a great deal over the last couple of years. Radical Pride is a much more intersectional march than the main Pride parade. You’ll find queer people from immigrant communities, sex workers, working-class people and many other groups represented there. At the time, I remember seeing just one person carrying Algerian flags. I walked over to introduce myself, and she became
one of the first people I photographed after meeting at a public event.

I was also reaching out in other ways. I worked with other organisations, met people through them, posted open calls online and connected with people that way too. Eventually, it became word-of-mouth through different communities. So, I didn’t want the project to revolve entirely around Ludovic-Mohamed and his world. That said, he was very central to the beginning because he introduced me to so many people. He connected me with organisations supporting queer migrants, including groups helping LGBTQ+ asylum seekers in France, and with colleagues and other people he’d met over the years. From there, I was able to build relationships with many more people myself.

The project really became an act of collaboration. You had to find people and build enough trust for them to allow you to photograph them. How did you approach developing those relationships?

I don’t take my camera out for quite a long time after meeting someone. I try to be very clear about what I’m doing because, when you’re working on a long-term project, you don’t necessarily know where the photographs are going to end up. You don’t know which images you’ll choose, whether there’ll be a book, or who might eventually publish the work. I always try to be honest about that and explain where the project is at when I meet someone. My practice is much more centred on listening than it is on directing people I photograph. Of course, everything we talk about informs the portrait that eventually gets made, but I spend much more time trying to establish a genuine connection. Because of the nature of the project, the conversation quickly becomes very personal. In most cases I’m meeting someone for the first time, and I think there’s something interesting about that. Sometimes it’s easier to open up to a stranger than it is to a close friend.

People were incredibly generous in sharing their stories with me. In some ways, it’s a bit like talking to a therapist – someone who isn’t part of your everyday life. We would spend hours talking about faith, identity and sexuality before ever making photographs. There’s a process to it, but I never really know where it’s going to lead. Sometimes we don’t make any photographs at all and arrange to meet again. Sometimes that second meeting never happens. Other times we photograph for two hours, and sometimes only for fifteen minutes.

What I found really beautiful was how willing people were to trust me with such intimate parts of their lives.

There’s a huge element of trust being placed in you.

Definitely. For many of the people I met, it was the first time they’d ever been able to speak these things out loud. I think that’s changing a little now because there are more books, more events and more representation in the media and in culture generally. In a way, the project became about creating a space that didn’t exist before.

In your project statement you ask, “How do we photograph the invisible?” Based on what you’ve said about spending time with people before photographing them, how did you go about answering that question?

I think the first question is whether or not someone wants to be recognised. There’s a difference between anonymity and invisibility, but there’s also a tension between the two that I’m trying to explore in the work. Sometimes anonymity is about protection. Invisibility, on the other hand, is about not being seen at all. In the case of queer Muslims, people sometimes refuse your existence because they don’t believe it’s possible for you to exist.

Then there’s another kind of tension around visibility and invisibility as immigrants in France. People notice you immediately because of your skin colour, your features or the way you dress, perhaps because you’re wearing visible religious signifiers. In that sense, you become hyper-visible. But at the same time, people only see the surface. They stop at that outer layer. You’re reduced to a category, put into a box or pushed to one side. I think that’s an experience many immigrants share.

Some people want to remain anonymous because they’re not out to their families, or sometimes they’re not even fully out to themselves. For some people, seeing themselves recognised in a photograph can be frightening – not only because of their family, but because of where they are personally.

So, the challenge became: how do you remove identifiable features without recreating the same act of erasure that’s already imposed by society, religion or family upon someone’s queerness? That’s the fragile balance I’ve been trying to explore photographically.

One thing that’s important to me is that, even if someone tells me they’re happy to be recognised, I’ll always make photographs where they aren’t identifiable as well. Partly that’s become an exercise in expanding my understanding of portraiture beyond photographing someone’s face. I want to tell stories in other ways. It’s also because I know how these decisions can change. Someone might leave a conversation feeling empowered and think, “I’m ready . Y ou can show my face.” Then, a few weeks later, they might feel differently. That’s happened several times. The reverse is true as well. If someone asks for anonymity, I’ll still make portraits where their face is visible – not for publication, but so I can give them photographs of
themselves for their private use or archive. They can keep them, share them with someone they love. Sometimes, months or even years later, someone will come back and say, “Actually , I feel ready now . Y ou can use the portrait where you can see my face.” I try to create space for both possibilities.

There are two photographs of Bouchta, one of your subjects, placed side by side. In one they are sitting on a sofa smoking a cigarette, and in the other they’re reflected in a mirror with a covering over their head. I’m interested in how you approached sequencing the book. Were there particular decisions or combinations of images that evolved as you developed the edit?

What did you think of those two photographs being next to each other?

I think they’re perfectly sequenced. They work beautifully together. There’s a duality there.

That pairing wasn’t my original idea, it was Sarah Chaplin Espenon, editor at Loose Joints. The mirror photograph had been my closing image for years. Whether I was making a book dummy or sequencing an exhibition, it almost always appeared at the end. Pairing the two images together was actually quite a recent decision. I think it works because it becomes a kind of revelation. The first image in the mirror came from a very playful moment. I think there was a curtain hanging nearby, and Bouchta draped it over her head. We experimented with lots of different ideas during that shoot. Then, when you turn the page, you’re actually looking at another photograph made in another mirror in her apartment. The doubling happens because the mirror itself has a slight angle to it. I love photographing through mirrors.

At the time I made those photographs, I was also thinking about this idea of doubling. Bouchta is someone who lives with many different identities, and I’ve spent a lot of time with her over the past five years whenever I’ve visited. There isn’t one simple answer to how she experiences her identity.

The doubling in those photographs can speak to the plural identities people hold as queer Muslims, as immigrants or as the children of immigrants. But in Bouchta’s case, it also speaks to the different parts of yourself that you have to live with internally.

It’s a beautiful image.

Thank you.

You mentioned your love of photographing through mirrors just now, but did you encounter any creative or practical challenges while making the project?

Well, my camera broke at one point and I lost about twenty rolls of film because I didn’t realise it hadn’t actually been exposing anything. That was a technical challenge…creatively, though, I actually enjoyed working within the constraints of the project. A lot of the photographs were made indoors. When I began the project I was very focused on photographing people inside their homes because those spaces felt important. It can be difficult to practise your faith or fully express yourself in public, or around family, whereas your bedroom or apartment becomes a place where you can be yourself without facing that discrimination.

I photographed almost everyone in their own space. That created practical limitations because many people lived in very small apartments. We were working entirely with window light, and because we always spent so long talking beforehand, we often ended up photographing during the last light of the day. Those constraints became part of the work. There was also one photograph – one of my favourites – that had to be removed from the project for about a year. The person in the photograph was going through a period of questioning and uncertainty. Although she wasn’t recognisable in the image, I felt I needed to let the photograph rest for a while. It’s the photograph of the hand coming out from behind the curtain. It was one of my favourite photographs, but I accepted that it shouldn’t be included in exhibitions or sequences for a while.

To that person, the photograph had become part of her own journey towards self-acceptance. Even though she couldn’t be identified, the image represented something very personal. It’s a strong photograph symbolically – someone emerging from behind the curtain, holding beads and reaching towards the light while still remaining partly hidden. It reflected everything she was experiencing at the time. She wasn’t ready for it to be part of the project. But, as her own life changed and she became more accepting of herself, she was happy for the image to be included again.

It’s a very powerful photograph. It was one of the first images I was drawn to when I looked through the book.

Thank you. There are around fifty people in the project, photographed over five years, and that’s a huge responsibility. Carrying those photographs and those stories into the world is as much a part of the work as making the pictures themselves.

For me, it’s just as important to make sure the people behind the photographs are protected as it is to make the photographs in the first place, and when someone didn’t want to be photographed, it became an opportunity to find another creative solution.

It certainly sounds as though trust sits at the centre of the project. With that in mind, many of the photographs almost become placeholders for the conversations you had with people. Do you think of the book primarily as a record, a meditation, or something else entirely?

I think meditation is probably closer. The book is really about emotion. It’s an emotional journey more than it is a documentary record. Of course, there are some portraits where you can clearly recognise someone and perhaps identify them as queer or Muslim. But many of the photographs don’t work that way. I became much more interested in recording emotional experiences.

Over the last five years I’ve shared so many different experiences with people – long conversations, singing prayers, deeply spiritual moments, crying together, laughing together. I’ve met people who were starting a family, who didn’t speak to their parents at the time, and then watched them introduce their children to their parents two years later. I’ve seen people move through evolving emotional journeys.

Those emotions are central because they’re about agency, which is about existence, which is about survival. What I wanted to capture were feelings that are almost impossible to understand unless you’ve lived them yourself. If someone spends time with the book, I hope they come away understanding that there is love, there is joy, there is spirituality, there is anger – there’s an entire emotional landscape. The sequencing of the book is really driven by those emotional movements.

Alongside these emotional movements, one of the things that comes across throughout the work is that visibility, community and simply living openly can become acts of resistance. What else do you hope people come to understand differently after spending time with the work?

The first thing I want the work to say is that these people can, and do, exist. I’m not trying to argue that there aren’t real problems. There are. I’m not trying to claim that Islam is somehow completely accepting of homosexuality. I’m trying to show that it is possible, and that within these communities I found so much beauty. At one point I even thought about converting because I was so moved by the faith, the love, and the sense of community I encountered.

So, first, the work is a statement of existence. Then, if you spend longer with it, I hope it becomes a statement of beauty. Above all, I hope it challenges the stereotypes people carry. The more we show that queer Muslim lives can be lives of love, beauty and community, the more we can challenge the discrimination that surrounds them. If we erase people’s existence, their experiences and their reasons for living authentically, then we’re only reinforcing that discrimination. I also hope that someone who is a queer Muslim, but who doesn’t yet have a community around them, might come across this book and recognise a part of themselves within it. Of course, I can’t change minds through art alone. People have to be willing to engage with it.

They can keep them, share them with someone they love. Sometimes, months or even years later, someone will come back and say, “Actually , I feel ready now . Y ou can use the portrait where you can see my face.” I try to create space for both possibilities. There are two photographs of Bouchta, one of your subjects, placed side by side. In one they are sitting on a sofa smoking a cigarette, and in the other they’re reflected in a mirror with a covering over their head. I’m interested in how you approached sequencing the book. Were there particular decisions or combinations of images that evolved as you developed the edit? What did you think of those two photographs being next to each other? I think they’re perfectly sequenced. They work beautifully together. There’s a duality there. That pairing wasn’t my original idea, it was Sarah Chaplin Espenon, editor at Loose Joints. The mirror photograph had been my closing image for years. Whether I was making a book dummy or sequencing an exhibition, it almost always appeared at the end. Pairing the two images together was actually quite a recent decision. I think it works because it becomes a kind of revelation. The first image in the mirror came from a very playful moment. I think there was a curtain hanging nearby, and Bouchta draped it over her head. We experimented with lots of different ideas during that shoot. Then, when you turn the page, you’re actually looking at another photograph made in another mirror in her apartment. The doubling happens because the mirror itself has a slight angle to it. I love photographing through mirrors. At the time I made those photographs, I was also thinking about this idea of doubling. Bouchta is someone who lives with many different identities, and I’ve spent a lot of time with her over the past five years whenever I’ve visited. There isn’t one simple answer to how she experiences her identity. The doubling in those photographs can speak to the plural identities people hold as queer Muslims, as immigrants or as the children of immigrants. But in Bouchta’s case, it also speaks to the different parts of yourself that you have to live with internally. It’s a beautiful image. Thank you. You mentioned your love of photographing through mirrors just now, but did you encounter any creative or practical challenges while making the project? Well, my camera broke at one point and I lost about twenty rolls of film because I didn’t realise it hadn’t actually been exposing anything. That was a technical challenge…creatively, though, I actually enjoyed working within the constraints of the project. A lot of the photographs were made indoors. When I began the project I was very focused on photographing people inside their homes because those spaces felt important. It can be difficult to practise your faith or fully express yourself in public, or around family, whereas your bedroom or apartment becomes a place where you can be yourself without facing that discrimination. I photographed almost everyone in their own space. That created practical limitations because many people lived in very small apartments. We were working entirely with window light, and because we always spent so long talking beforehand, we often ended up photographing during the last light of the day. Those constraints became part of the work. There was also one photograph – one of my favourites – that had to be removed from the project for about a year. The person in the photograph was going through a period of questioning and uncertainty. Although she wasn’t recognisable in the image, I felt I needed to let the photograph rest for a while. It’s the photograph of the hand coming out from behind the curtain. It was one of my favourite photographs, but I accepted that it shouldn’t be included in exhibitions or sequences for a while. To that person, the photograph had become part of her own journey towards self-acceptance. Even though she couldn’t be identified, the image represented something very personal. It’s a strong photograph symbolically – someone emerging from behind the curtain, holding beads and reaching towards the light while still remaining partly hidden. It reflected everything she was experiencing at the time. She wasn’t ready for it to be part of the project. But, as her own life changed and she became more accepting of herself, she was happy for the image to be included again. It’s a very powerful photograph. It was one of the first images I was drawn to when I looked through the book. Thank you. There are around fifty people in the project, photographed over five years, and that’s a huge responsibility. Carrying those photographs and those stories into the world is as much a part of the work as making the pictures themselves. For me, it’s just as important to make sure the people behind the photographs are protected as it is to make the photographs in the first place, and when someone didn’t want to be photographed, it became an opportunity to find another creative solution. It certainly sounds as though trust sits at the centre of the project. With that in mind, many of the photographs almost become placeholders for the conversations you had with people. Do you think of the book primarily as a record, a meditation, or something else entirely? I think meditation is probably closer. The book is really about emotion. It’s an emotional journey more than it is a documentary record. Of course, there are some portraits where you can clearly recognise someone and perhaps identify them as queer or Muslim. But many of the photographs don’t work that way. I became much more interested in recording emotional experiences. Over the last five years I’ve shared so many different experiences with people – long conversations, singing prayers, deeply spiritual moments, crying together, laughing together. I’ve met people who were starting a family, who didn’t speak to their parents at the time, and then watched them introduce their children to their parents two years later. I’ve seen people move through evolving emotional journeys. Those emotions are central because they’re about agency, which is about existence, which is about survival. What I wanted to capture were feelings that are almost impossible to understand unless you’ve lived them yourself. If someone spends time with the book, I hope they come away understanding that there is love, there is joy, there is spirituality, there is anger – there’s an entire emotional landscape. The sequencing of the book is really driven by those emotional movements. Alongside these emotional movements, one of the things that comes across throughout the work is that visibility, community and simply living openly can become acts of resistance. What else do you hope people come to understand differently after spending time with the work? The first thing I want the work to say is that these people can, and do, exist. I’m not trying to argue that there aren’t real problems. There are. I’m not trying to claim that Islam is somehow completely accepting of homosexuality. I’m trying to show that it is possible, and that within these communities I found so much beauty. At one point I even thought about converting because I was so moved by the faith, the love, and the sense of community I encountered. So, first, the work is a statement of existence. Then, if you spend longer with it, I hope it becomes a statement of beauty. Above all, I hope it challenges the stereotypes people carry. The more we show that queer Muslim lives can be lives of love, beauty and community, the more we can challenge the discrimination that surrounds them. If we erase people’s existence, their experiences and their reasons for living authentically, then we’re only reinforcing that discrimination. I also hope that someone who is a queer Muslim, but who doesn’t yet have a community around them, might come across this book and recognise a part of themselves within it. Of course, I can’t change minds through art alone. People have to be willing to engage with it. Acerca de Camille Farrah Lenain

Camille Farrah Lenain (b. 1990) es un fotógrafo y educador francés-algeriano con sede entre Nueva Orleans y Nueva York. Explorando identidad, memoria y pertenencia, su trabajo desafía la concepción social centrando comunidades y experiencias que resisten narrativas simplistas. Su práctica combina investigación inmersiva, retrato y sonido, creando trabajo que amplifica las voces a menudo pasadas por alto o malinterpretadas.

Estudió fotografía en l’ESA en Bruselas y en el Centro Internacional de Fotografía en Nueva York. Sus fotografías han sido exhibidas en instituciones y festivales en todo el mundo, incluyendo el Arab World Institute, Ogden Museum of Southern Art and Photoville. En 2024, fue reconocida con el Premio Arnold Newman de Nuevas Direcciones en Portraitura Fotográfica, el Premio Leica Women Photo y el Centro de Creadores de Apertura de la Universidad Mitchell

Prefacio

Comenzando como un acto personal de recuerdo y carta de amor a su tío, Farid, Made of Smokeless Fire evolucionó en un retrato colectivo de la vida musulmana reinante en Francia. En lugar de tratar de explicar o definir sus temas, las fotografías de Camille Farrah Lenain navegan por el espacio frágil entre la visibilidad y el anonimato, preguntando cómo el retrato podría representar vidas que tan a menudo se suponen no existir.

Entrevista

Hecho de fuego sin humo comenzó como un acto de recuerdo, y usted ha descrito el proyecto como una carta de amor a su tío, Farid. ¿Podría usted decirme un poco más sobre su relación con él y cómo moldeó el trabajo?

Mi familia es francesa-algeriana. Ellos emigraron a Francia en los años 50, y yo vengo de una gran familia – mis abuelos tenían nueve hijos. Parte de la familia vivía en París: mi madre, mi tío y mis tías. Crecí mayormente en París, así que eran la gente con la que pasé los fines de semana, cumpleaños y cenas familiares. Todavía lo son. Mi tío era una parte central de ese grupo.

Él simplemente murió en 2013, y ese fue un momento muy difícil para nuestra familia. Yo ya había perdido a otros dos tíos antes de morir, pero su muerte fue particularmente difícil porque él era uno de los más jóvenes de mis abuelos nueve hijos. Él era el pegamento que mantenía a nuestra familia juntos. Él siempre se rió, haciendo chistes, burlando a todos. Él era el favorito de todos. Creo que se le permite decir que una vez que alguien ha pasado unos años

Debido a que estaba enfermo con el SIDA durante los años noventa, su diagnóstico casi se convirtió en una forma de salir. Por supuesto, no todos con SIDA eran gays, pero en ese momento a menudo significaba que las familias se enfrentaban a conversaciones que no habían tenido antes. Quería entender lo que su vida había sido como un hombre árabe en Francia, y lo que la comunidad gay en París había sido como para él. Tenía curiosidad por su relación con Dios y cómo reconcilió la fe homosexualidad.

Cuando traté de hablar de todo esto con mi madre y mis tías, realmente no recibí ninguna respuesta. No creo que estuvieran listos para hablar de ello ya que el dolor todavía era demasiado pesado. Eventualmente, llegué a un gay francés-algeriano Imam viviendo en Marsella que era VIH positivo que había oído hablar. Él me invitó a pasar tiempo con él y un grupo de queer musulmanes en Marsella retiro.

De esas primeras conversaciones en Marsella, ¿cómo evoluciona el proyecto más allá de la historia de tu tío en un retrato colectivo de la vida musulmana reinante en Francia?

Creo que realmente sucedió durante ese fin de semana y durante el curso de ese verano. Fue una gran entrada en este mundo. Pasé cuatro días con un grupo de alrededor de diez o quince personas, participando en diferentes actividades, teniendo conversaciones y mostrando fotografías de mi tío mientras contaba su historia.

Al principio, yo estaba tratando de relacionar todo de nuevo con él. La gente miraba sus fotografías y decía, “Me recuerda a mi hermano”, o “Siento que lo conozco”. En ese sentido, se convirtió en el pegamento que reunió a toda esta gente. Siempre ha permanecido central en el proyecto y en esas conversaciones. Todo lo que he fotografiado ha visto una fotografía de mi tío o me ha oído hablar de él.

Parte de este trabajo es sobre desafiar el estigma y los estereotipos que rodean vidas musulmanas queer. A menudo se les dice que no pueden existir. Hay esta suposición generalizada de que, si usted es maricón, usted será inevitablemente rechazado por su religión, su familia y su comunidad – que el Islam es de alguna manera la peor religión en la que ser maricón. No creo que eso sea totalmente cierto. Todos son complicados. Cada religión tiene sus propias tensiones y contradicciones.

Lo que comenzó como una manera de entender la historia de mi tío gradualmente se convirtió en entender una cuestión mucho más grande que tantas personas estaban navegando. Después de un año o dos, también me interesó mucho más en la religión misma. Al principio, estaba pensando realmente a través de la cultura musulmana porque se relacionaba con mi propia familia y experiencia árabe. Más tarde, me interesé cada vez más en la relación más amplia entre la alegría y la fe, y que expandió el proyecto aún más.

Creo que, en última instancia, se trataba de entender que no hay una sola historia. Me comprometí profundamente a escuchar los matices de la experiencia de cada persona. Hay hilos que conectan a todos, pero juntos forman una web mucho más grande.

Este retiro en Marsella. ¿Podrías contarme un poco más sobre eso?

Sí. Fue organizado por un instituto llamado CALEM y Ludovic-Mohamed Zahed, el Imam que mencioné anteriormente. Congregó a personas de toda Francia, e incluso más allá. Por ejemplo, había alguien allí que había viajado desde Canadá y era originario de Pakistán. El retiro también estaba relacionado con otras organizaciones de Marsella, incluyendo una organización que apoya a migrantes LGBTQ+.

Durante el retiro, compartimos comidas juntos, oramos juntos y participamos en diferentes actividades. Celebramos discusiones y tuvimos reuniones sociales. También pasamos tiempo juntos por la ciudad, salimos bailando y disfrutando de estar juntos.

¿Era específicamente para los musulmanes LGBTQ+, o estaba abierto a personas de todos los ámbitos de la vida?

Era específicamente para los musulmanes LGBTQ+ y sus aliados. También había un sacerdote gay allí, por ejemplo, que era abiertamente acogedor de los musulmanes queer, y compartió sus propias experiencias y perspectiva desde un punto de vista cristiano.

Eso es fantástico.

Realmente fue increíble.

He estado leyendo un poco acerca de Ludovic-Mohamed Zahed – usted lo mencionó justo ahora. Con esos primeros encuentros, ¿Formó el trabajo? ¿En realidad esas reuniones se movió el proyecto?

Sí, definitivamente. A través de su investigación y a través de la gente que conocí en ese retiro, el proyecto realmente comenzó a tomar forma. Ludovic-Mohamed es muy un erudito, pero mi fondo no es académico por lo que no estaba cómodo, ni interesado en acercarme a él de esta manera. Lo importante para mí era la comunidad que se reunió alrededor de él, porque me permitió conocer a tantas personas diferentes. Él era ciertamente influyente en el principio, pero también no quería ser completamente fuera de su proyecto.

Ese mismo año fui al Orgullo Radical en París. Hace seis años, se veía muy diferente de hoy. Había muy poca representación visible de los musulmanes y árabes queer, aunque creo que eso ha cambiado mucho en los últimos dos años. El Orgullo Radical es una marcha mucho más interseccional que el principal desfile del Orgullo. Encontrarás gente queer de comunidades inmigrantes, trabajadores sexuales, gente de clase obrera y muchos otros grupos allí representados.
una de las primeras personas que fotografié después de reunirse en un evento público.

También estaba llegando de otras maneras. Trabajé con otras organizaciones, conocí a gente a través de ellas, publicó llamadas abiertas en línea y conectadas con personas de esa manera. Eventualmente, se convirtió en palabra de boca a través de diferentes comunidades. Por lo tanto, no quería que el proyecto girara por completo alrededor de Ludovic-Mohamed y su mundo. Eso dijo, él era muy central al principio porque él me presentó a tantas personas.

El proyecto realmente se convirtió en un acto de colaboración. Tenías que encontrar gente y construir suficiente confianza para que te permitiera fotografiarlos. ¿Cómo te acercaste a desarrollar esas relaciones?

No abro mi cámara durante mucho tiempo después de conocer a alguien. Trato de ser muy claro acerca de lo que estoy haciendo porque, cuando estás trabajando en un proyecto a largo plazo, no necesariamente sabes dónde van a terminar las fotografías. No sabes qué imágenes elegirás, si habrá un libro o quién podría publicar el trabajo. Siempre intento ser honesto acerca de eso y explicar dónde está el proyecto.

La gente era increíblemente generosa en compartir sus historias conmigo. De alguna manera, es un poco como hablar con un terapeuta – alguien que no es parte de su vida cotidiana. Pasamos horas hablando de fe, identidad y sexualidad antes de hacer fotografías. Hay un proceso para ello, pero nunca realmente sé dónde va a liderar. A veces no hacemos ninguna fotografía y arreglamos para reunirse de nuevo. Otras veces ese segundo encuentro nunca sucede.

Lo que encontré realmente hermoso era lo dispuesto que la gente estaba para confiar en mí con partes tan íntimas de sus vidas.

Hay un enorme elemento de confianza en ser colocado en usted.

Definitivamente. Para muchas de las personas que conocí, fue la primera vez que pudieron hablar estas cosas en voz alta. Creo que eso está cambiando un poco ahora porque hay más libros, más eventos y más representación en los medios y en la cultura en general. De alguna manera, el proyecto se convirtió en crear un espacio que no existía antes.

En su declaración de proyecto pregunta: “¿Cómo fotografiamos lo invisible?” Basado en lo que has dicho sobre pasar tiempo con la gente antes de fotografiarlos, ¿cómo has ido a responder esa pregunta?

Creo que la primera pregunta es si alguien quiere o no ser reconocido. Hay una diferencia entre el anonimato y la invisibilidad, pero también hay una tensión entre los dos que estoy tratando de explorar en el trabajo. A veces el anonimato es sobre protección. La invisibilidad, por otro lado, es sobre no ser vista en absoluto. En el caso de los musulmanes queer, la gente a veces rechaza su existencia porque no cree que exista.

Luego hay otro tipo de tensión alrededor de la visibilidad y la invisibilidad como inmigrantes en Francia. La gente le notan inmediatamente debido a su color de piel, sus características o la forma de vestir, tal vez porque usted está usando signos religiosos visibles. En ese sentido, usted se vuelve hipervisible. Pero al mismo tiempo, la gente sólo ve la superficie. Se detienen en esa capa exterior. Usted se reduce a una categoría, se pone en una caja o empuja a un lado.

Algunas personas quieren permanecer anónimos porque no están fuera de sus familias, o a veces no están totalmente fuera de sí mismos. Para algunas personas, al verse reconocidos en una fotografía puede ser aterrador – no sólo por su familia, sino por donde son personalmente.

Así, el desafío se convirtió: ¿cómo se eliminan las características identificables sin recrear el mismo acto de borrado que ya está impuesto por la sociedad, la religión o la familia sobre la desconfianza de alguien? Ese es el frágil equilibrio que he estado tratando de explorar fotográficamente.

Una cosa que es importante para mí es que, incluso si alguien me dice que están felices de ser reconocidos, siempre haré fotografías donde no son identificables también. Parte que se ha convertido en un ejercicio en la expansión de mi comprensión de retrato más allá de fotografiar la cara de alguien. Quiero contar historias de otras maneras. También es porque sé cómo estas decisiones pueden cambiar. Alguien puede dejar una conversación sintiéndose empoderada y pensar,
ellos mismos para su uso privado o archivo. Ellos pueden guardarlos, compartirlos con alguien que aman. A veces, meses o incluso años después, alguien volverá y dirá, "En realidad, me siento listo ahora. Y ou puede usar el retrato donde puedes ver mi cara." Trato de crear espacio para ambas posibilidades.

Hay dos fotografías de Bouchta, uno de tus súbditos, colocado lado a lado. En uno están sentados en un sofá fumando un cigarrillo, y en el otro se reflejan en un espejo con una cubierta sobre su cabeza. Me interesa cómo te acercaste a secuenciar el libro. ¿Existen decisiones o combinaciones particulares de imágenes que evolucionaron a medida que desarrollaste la edición?

¿Qué pensaste de que esas dos fotografías estaban al lado del otro?

Creo que están perfectamente secuenciados. Trabajan muy bien juntos. Hay una dualidad allí.

Ese pareado no fue mi idea original, fue Sarah Chaplin Espenon, editora de Loose Joints. La fotografía del espejo había sido mi imagen de cierre durante años. Ya sea que estaba haciendo un borrador de libro o secuenciando una exposición, casi siempre apareció al final. Pareciendo las dos imágenes juntas era realmente una decisión bastante reciente. Creo que funciona porque se convierte en una especie de revelación.

En el momento en que hice esas fotografías, también estaba pensando en esta idea de duplicar. Bouchta es alguien que vive con muchas identidades diferentes, y he pasado mucho tiempo con ella durante los últimos cinco años cuando he visitado. No hay una simple respuesta a cómo ella experimenta su identidad.

La duplicación en esas fotografías puede hablar de las identidades plurales que tienen las personas como musulmanes queer, como inmigrantes o como hijos de inmigrantes. Pero en el caso de Bouchta, también habla a las diferentes partes de ti mismo que tienes que vivir internamente.

Es una imagen hermosa.

Gracias.

Usted mencionó su amor de fotografiar a través de espejos justo ahora, pero ¿encontraste algún desafío creativo o práctico al hacer el proyecto?

Bueno, mi cámara se rompió en un momento y perdí alrededor de veinte carretes porque no me di cuenta de que no había estado exponiendo nada. Eso fue un reto técnico...creativamente, sin embargo, realmente disfruté trabajando dentro de las limitaciones del proyecto. Muchas de las fotografías fueron hechas en interiores. Cuando empecé el proyecto estaba muy centrado en fotografiar a la gente dentro de sus hogares porque esos espacios se sentían importantes.

Fotografié a casi todo el mundo en su propio espacio. Eso creó limitaciones prácticas porque mucha gente vivía en apartamentos muy pequeños. Trabajamos totalmente con luz de ventana, y porque siempre pasamos tanto tiempo hablando de antemano, a menudo terminamos fotografiando durante la última luz del día. Esas limitaciones se convirtieron en parte de la obra. También había una fotografía – uno de mis favoritos – que tenía que ser quitada del proyecto durante un año.

Para esa persona, la fotografía se había convertido en parte de su propio viaje hacia la autoaceptación. Aunque no podía ser identificada, la imagen representaba algo muy personal. Es una fotografía fuerte simbólicamente – alguien emergente de detrás de la cortina, sujetando cuentas y alcanzando hacia la luz mientras todavía permanecía en parte oculta. Reflejó todo lo que estaba experimentando en el momento. Ella no estaba lista para que fuera parte del proyecto.

Es una fotografía muy poderosa. Fue una de las primeras imágenes a las que me atrajo cuando miré a través del libro.

Gracias. Hay alrededor de cincuenta personas en el proyecto, fotografiadas durante cinco años, y eso es una gran responsabilidad. Llevar esas fotografías y esas historias en el mundo es tanto una parte del trabajo como hacer las fotos ellos mismos.

Para mí, es tan importante asegurarse de que la gente detrás de las fotografías esté protegida como para hacer las fotografías en primer lugar, y cuando alguien no quería ser fotografiado, se convirtió en una oportunidad para encontrar otra solución creativa.

Sin duda suena como si la confianza se sienta en el centro del proyecto. Con eso en mente, muchas de las fotografías casi se convierten en titulares de lugares para las conversaciones que tuvieron con la gente. ¿Piensas en el libro principalmente como un registro, una meditación, o algo más por completo?

Creo que la meditación es probablemente más cercana. El libro es realmente sobre la emoción. Es un viaje emocional más de lo que es un registro documental. Por supuesto, hay algunos retratos donde se puede reconocer claramente a alguien y quizás identificarlos como mariscal o musulmán. Pero muchas de las fotografías no funcionan de esa manera. Me interesó mucho más en grabar experiencias emocionales.

Durante los últimos cinco años he compartido tantas experiencias diferentes con la gente – largas conversaciones, oraciones cantando, momentos profundamente espirituales, llorando juntos, riendo juntos. He conocido a gente que estaba empezando una familia, que no habló con sus padres en ese momento, y luego los vi introducir a sus hijos a sus padres dos años más tarde. He visto a la gente moverse a través de viajes emocionales en evolución.

Esas emociones son centrales porque se trata de la agencia, que se trata de la existencia, que se trata de la supervivencia. Lo que quería capturar eran sentimientos que son casi imposibles de entender a menos que los hayas vivido tú mismo. Si alguien pasa tiempo con el libro, espero que vengan a entender que hay amor, hay alegría, hay espiritualidad, hay enojo – hay un paisaje emocional entero. La secuenciación del libro es realmente impulsada por esos movimientos emocionales.

Junto a estos movimientos emocionales, una de las cosas que se encuentran a lo largo del trabajo es que la visibilidad, la comunidad y simplemente vivir abiertamente pueden convertirse en actos de resistencia. ¿Qué más esperas que la gente llegue a entender de manera diferente después de pasar tiempo con el trabajo?

Lo primero que quiero decir es que estas personas pueden, y sí existen. No estoy tratando de argumentar que no hay problemas reales. Hay. No estoy tratando de afirmar que el Islam está de alguna manera totalmente aceptando la homosexualidad. Estoy tratando de demostrar que es posible, y que dentro de estas comunidades he encontrado tanta belleza. En un momento incluso pensé en convertir porque estaba tan movido por la fe, el amor y la comunidad que encontré.

Así que, primero, la obra es una declaración de existencia. Entonces, si pasas más tiempo con ella, espero que se convierta en una declaración de belleza. Sobre todo, espero que desafía a los estereotipos que la gente lleva. Cuanto más mostramos que las vidas musulmanas pueden ser vidas de amor, belleza y comunidad, más podemos desafiar la discriminación que los rodea. Si borramos la existencia de la gente, sus experiencias y sus razones para vivir auténticamente, entonces reconozco que la discriminación es sólo eso.

About Olivia Bee 2026

Olivia Bee is a photographer and director. She is intrigued by the magic of everyday life, a human’s inherent connection with land, the duality of love, and how the beauty of memories (real or imagined) touches us.

She became the youngest artist to have a book published with Aperture Foundation with the release of her monograph “Kids In Love” at 22 years old in 2016. The work was shown as a solo show at Aperture Foundation as well as agnès b in New York City. She has been included in group exhibitions with Danziger Gallery, agnès b, Aperture Foundation, Weinstein Gallery, Bernal Espacio Galeria, and with Van Cleef & Arpels in Kyoto and Paris. Olivia lives in Southwestern Oregon with her husband, Joe, and their daughter, Mary. They run Y Knot Farm + Ranch in Oregon’s Umpqua Valley, with a focus on regenerative, pasture raised meats. Foreword

What a joy, to watch a photographer grow and evolve. We've been following the work of Olivia Bee since she started on Flickr. We first interviewed her in 2014, when she was based in NY, then again in 2018 when she'd moved to Los Angeles, and had planned to make it a more regular occurrence...but we all know how 2022 went...

Took awhile, but we finally got to sit down with Olivia, now in Oregon, in another phase of work and life. Still creating, still growing, still very much herself.

----

Interview

We’ll jump right in. What’s changed since we last interviewed you, eight years ago? Easy one.

So much! I live in rural america now, I run a farm with my husband. I’m married. I have a child.

I feel like I grew up in the city not knowing that some things were an option. I never knew that you could live in rural America or that you could have a horse. I just thought that was something you were born into and you couldn’t choose that. But, you know, there were always inklings of this kind of stuff when I was a little kid. We were always gardening and my parents had a big yard. We were always outside and I was always really interested in, say, the tomato that came from the garden. It’s all been  a road map back to myself. I feel like that’s especially evident when you have a kid, I’m remembering all these things that got me excited as a kid and seeing myself through new eyes. Coming back to myself in ways that maybe I didn’t expect but feel very natural.

Yeah, most importantly though, how goes the work? Babies are nice and all, but what about photography!

It’s good! I just want to make the most magical childhood for my daughter. And so that ends up being in pictures because I’m always photographing what I’m going through in my life and what’s happening, whether that’s an external circumstance or observation or an internal monologue or fantasy. I’ve been photographing our life on the farm, but with this new magical inclination. I’m being drawn to making costumes and making little houses out of papier-mâché, growing just like a shit ton of flowers so that my daughter can be in a field of flowers. My life comes first, my photographs come second, but my photographs are always evidence of that life, or proof. It comes from life first and it’s always been that way. So it’s good. I’m shooting more commercial work, which is really fun. I feel like I need it. It’s generative for me to go out and be creative for other people and get paid and go on a trip. To have to deal with all these challenges that come with shooting commercially and then bring that hustle back to my home and seeing things with a new set of eyes because I was just in a different setting. They inform each other.

How does the professional field feel for you? The last few years have been very tumultuous for people in photography.

There’s a lot to be afraid of. And I try not to go there, because then I can’t get out. With AI, you know, some people’s careers are just over, if you don’t pivot, it’s going to be gone. There’s this push, the world’s going in two different directions in terms of visuals, there’s the super-obvious, “perfect AI can do this, why wouldn’t we have AI do this?” Then there’s this whole real attraction to human imperfection. And I’ve always been attracted to human imperfection and how that makes things beautiful. So I’m diving into that even more. Because I don’t think that can be replaced with AI, I think AI is does a great job at, unfortunately, things like e-commerce, and which I think people should be still shooting as a job, I don’t think we need to save j crew, like, tons of money, and the thing I don’t get about AI is, do you not realize that if all the jobs of the people who buy your things are gone, you won’t be able to sell your shit. You need all those blue collar white collar people to buy your dumb t shirts.

It’s part of the ecosystem.

Yeah, exactly. They’re not thinking about that. They’re thinking about cutting their numbers, not like, where’s our consumer going to be? And you see people struggling to, I mean, obviously, gas right now. Just doing life is a lot more expensive than it used to be. But people seem to be paid less, across the board, not just in the photography industry, I think in general, no raises yet your taxes go up, gas is more expensive, groceries
are more, just everything’s more expensive. All that to say, I’m choosing to be optimistic. And that people will always want a human touch. And I feel like there’s always going to be doom and gloom. It’s pretty tense.

In our industry, you can always be like, “well, it wasn’t like the 80s. Well, it wasn’t like the early 2000s.” And so I try to think in terms of, okay, what in 20 years are people going to be like, “God, I wish I could go back to that. It wasn’t like it was in 2026.” Which sounds crazy to say out loud, but what are those avenues to develop in and try to pivot under? There’s still ad work, but it’s definitely different. I’m trying to go for things that I maybe I didn’t shoot when I was younger. I think it’s either adapt or migrate or die. So it’s hard staying where you are and wishing things were different, it’s hard changing and figuring out how to be present and current…you choose your hard.

Part of that too, is surrounding myself with positive people. People who recognize the difficulties in the industry, but want to keep going and want to
find the good in it. People are always going to need a human touch, people always going to want human stories, or at least the world I want to live in and the world I want for my daughter. And even if that world is maybe less than the whole world, I think it’s still going to be there.

Do you feel like you’ve got a balance right now between like your art and your life?

I feel like I have a balance between my art and my life but it’s an ever-evolving dance, especially with the seasonality of farm work. Admittedly, I’m not doing as much of the manual labor as I used to because I’m the primary caregiver and joe has to be on the tractor a lot, but I feel so lucky for Mary, too, because we’re both able to be home. She gets to be with us 24-7.

When you’re a mom you’ve become a little more efficient with your time or maybe inefficient in other ways, but like, “okay I have 15 minutes while she’s playing with blocks or asleep or is really into this book, I better make the most of this 15 minutes because I’m gonna want to be with her
after when she’s not focused on something else or if she’s not sleeping.” It’s a challenge. Commercial stuff is not usually on schedule. My schedule is based on her schedule and then hopefully other things fit into it or I have to figure it out. I’d like to be working more, I would love to be doing a shoot a month, I think i’m headed back to that. Everything’s how it’s supposed to be. Also, it’s so beautiful here right now, it’s like this every day for months so it’s not a bad time to be home…but I have a big job in two weeks. So I’m excited for that.

I used to be like, “I wish I could only do my personal work and not do any commercial work.” And I did that. And it really sucks to be a starving artist. It sucks. I wasn’t creative, because I was in survival mode, and I know a lot of people can relate to that. I was literally just thinking, “how are we going to make these next bill payments?” I’m not thinking, “oh, it’d be great if I turned into a butterfly today.” It gave me a lot of perspective, because when I started taking pictures, I was still a dependent of my parents, and I was working that way. I got to really explore what I wanted to say and how I wanted to shoot without the pressure of making money.

Why is it that you think your career has survived when other people seem to be floundering?

I don’t think it came without floundering, I’ve definitely had moments of floundering or thinking, “is this floundering?” or, “floundering is coming.” I’m definitely lucky, in a way. I’m always trying to…yeah, I’ll take a million pictures of myself in a field at sunset, but I am trying to do new things, too.

I don’t try to follow trends. I try to figure out what’s next for me and what’s interesting to me and hopefully that changes. I realized after Kids in Love and after I moved to rural America, “okay, I can’t be hired for kids having fun out in the world forever, because I’m not going to be a kid out in the world having fun forever.” I look at Rihanna, she’s evolved so many times. And she does stuff on her own timeline. I’m always thinking, “okay, what would Rihanna do? She’d probably do something different. She’d probably try something new, but still be herself.” And she’s so unapologetically herself, even when it’s new or different.

Are you still using large format right now?

Not really. It’s too expensive. I’m sure I will return to it. I was also craving something between large format and 35mm, so I’ve been shooting mostly medium format and trying to marry those two worlds. I wanted a quicker way of image-making. I had a self-timer I’d had made by this robotics company to take pictures with my large format…but they didn’t last that long. So then I was always asking Joe, “can you please help me take a picture??” He’s always willing, of course. But I got into taking self-portraits because of the autonomy. So self-timer is my best friend, mainly with a Mamiya, most of the time. I mean, I still sprinkle in 35mm, even if it’s just disposable cameras. I always have one in my bag, but mostly Mamiya.

How is it being married to another photographer?

Oh, it’s cool. Joe is the kind of artist that won’t make something for a year and then he’ll go and make the most beautiful picture and I’m
almost like, “fuck you. ” I have to be fully available and taking pictures all the time to keep that muscle alive and well and I feel like he can just turn it on and be like, “ah, I’m back.” But it’s great. We have a lot to talk about, photo-wise. We have the same interests, agriculture and photography,
but I would say he’s more interested in agriculture than I am, and I’m more interested in photography than he is, it’s a nice balance.

I love that he loves image-making and sometimes he makes these pictures that make me think, “oh my god, how did you even get that?” And he gets it so fast.  I’ve been told I’m a pretty fast shooter by many people and I’m like, “you have not seen my husband.” The gut feeling, he is so good at just trusting that and coming out of this quiet time I had in my working life is a return to trusting in that gut feeling. He reminds me a lot that that’s my most important asset.

Have your inspirations changed over the past few years?

Yeah, I would say the list has gotten shorter. I’m looking to the ground a lot more because my kid’s down there. And I’m noticing bugs. And really, I have a macro lens now that I love. And I was like, “why did I never have a macro lens? This is so fun, seeing the world so small.” Sometimes I just use it for a portrait, but you can see the pores on the skin and I just…I used to be really interested in the landscape of the body and sensuality. And now I’m really interested in the landscape of the close-up, the close-up of my daughter’s eyes or my hair on her face or
how the water drips off of her hair, small things like that.

Details.

Yeah, small details become the landscape. I was just so interested in the body in a landscape and the body becoming the landscape. And yeah, now it’s the details. It’s kind of the opposite of what Sally Mann talks about when her work, when she was shooting immediate family, and then she went into her landscape stuff, her children were still in the pictures, and then she kept zooming out. So it was way more the landscape than the pictures and than the children and the children disappeared all together, but I feel it’s the opposite for me. Maybe that’s because I became a mother much further into my photographic journey than she did.

I also I had a very close friend of mine die, a year and a half ago now. And she respected all living beings down to like, the dung beetle, you know, and so I’ve been more appreciative of that, while we while she was here with us, but also after she died.

Is there work you’re excited to make in the future?

Oh, I mean always. I’m making a film. So that is very exciting. It might take a minute, but I’m making a film. A full length.

You did a short about dog sled racing.

Yeah, I did a short about about mushing, a short doc. I did my narrative short about the dancer, I’ve done plenty of music videos and things but definitely always craved doing something longer, so I’m excited about that.

Is this one you’ve written yourself as well?

Currently writing, yeah. It’s always about personal experiences, but made a little bit more palatable.

How often are you taking pictures right now?

I take a picture every day, sometimes that’s on my phone, and maybe it’s not something I’m going to put in a gallery, but it’s still using my visual brain. I go out to take pictures once a week, maybe twice a week. It depends on the weather, I get really inspired when it’s so lush and green outside and there’s rainbows and sometimes it’s raining and sometimes sunny and there’s flowers. You can be outside, not wearing a coat and you can sit on the ground. So, I’ll probably be taking more pictures now and then sometimes in the winter, less.

Have you considered doing other shows, other books?

For sure. I had a show last summer and books are how I think about pictures, it’s always a chapter of a book, but it’s such a thing to get them published. I think a book is warranted, but there’s nothing in the works right now. I’m always shooting for the next show and the next book so there there will be one.

Do you see the chapters of your life clearly?

Absolutely. In the pictures and the way I was taking pictures, oh yeah.

How do you articulate those chapters to yourself?

In a chapter of your life, what are the things you’re returning to? There are usually common themes, like, birds were really speaking to me then and I always wore this dress or whatever. It can seem like a superficial thing, but I think about it like, okay, if there’s a character in a movie that’s always wearing a red dress and suddenly she’s wearing a green dress, you think, okay, there’s something happening there and I feel like it’s the same in my life. It can come through clothing, it can come through a certain camera and how that makes you look at things a little differently. I get married to a camera for five years and then I move on. I don’t have to articulate it visually, it just happens, it’s not something I have to think about too hard. There are the common themes that I always come back to, you know, the body and the landscape, connection between people, pink, eggs, life and death, etc.

When I think of your career, the chapters of your work, it feels very city-based for me, there’s the early Portland period, then there’s the New York period, then there’s the LA period and there’s the return to Oregon period.

Totally, I think that’s accurate. The pictures that don’t resonate with me anymore are, yeah, the LA and New York pictures. I just like the pictures I’ve taken in Oregon. I like some of them, and I like certain projects I did. I think it’s more…maybe I just didn’t like my life as much. I liked the projects I
would go shoot and seek out, but when I was documenting my everyday life, which is such a life force for me and my creativity. I mean, I had a nice life. I had a great life, but it wasn’t deeply inspiring to me. The professional work was inspiring.

There’s a reason you came back to Oregon. It was a journey for you, where you had to have these other adventures to come back to Oregon.

Absolutely. I think about it in terms of place as well, that’s an inherent change of scenery, and an indicator that something has changed because it’s very obvious something has changed!

And there there is no anticipating what the next chapter is going to be?

No, I can imagine, there’ll be more kids, we’ll definitely have one more. We might not stay in Oregon forever, we want to figure that out before Mary is school age.

Where would you want to go?

Probably Montana or Wyoming and have a more Western way of life. We don’t want to be chicken farming forever. Joe is a horse boy, he’s ridden horses his whole life. He’s a champion in endurance riding. We have his horse, we have my horse, but he doesn’t want to go trail ride anymore and we want to be working with animals.

What we have here is wonderful, there are amazing people, it’s close to a lot of amenities. I’m not ready to leave, yet, but I imagine a world where we’re more in the wild. We want to be ranching rather than farming. Yeah, we’ve got a little time. But it goes by really quick, really quick.

More horse photos is what you really want.

Yeah! More horse photos. I always wanted to have an artist retreat when I lived in Eastern Oregon. That was kind of the plan, but then COVID hit and the place wasn’t really big enough for that. Maybe I could host a workshop or two, or a dinner, but we really want to have a dedicated place for artist retreats and also maybe a ranching school, because agriculture is dying in the US. It’s getting so much worse and young people can’t afford it, including us. You know, we have good other jobs and it’s so expensive.

So thinking about something like that in the long term and also, I want a studio that’s separate from the house, we’re just thinking about things that would make a dream thing. And then also maybe some multi-generational living, probably closer to his family, because his parents are both retired and more available for helping with kids.

It seems like you have a lot of ideas that seem possible to you, as grim as things can be.

You have to think it’s possible or it won’t happen. Joe is a big dreamer and I’m a big dreamer who’s also a realist. We’ve had to meet each other in the middle, like, “okay, let’s dream, I can dream bigger but it also needs to be able to happen.” We’re crazy like that and also a good team, but I don’t think other people understand our decision-making, which is fine, only we need to understand our decision-making.

It’s all seemed to really come together.

It always does, maybe it takes a second, but it always does.

Yeah, you’ve always seemed both aspirational and grounded.

That’s the balance of living on a farm and working with my hands and also going to LA to go shoot Kesha or whatever it is. I need that sparkle, but also that rootedness and, honestly, that shit. I deal with poop every day. I need that, but also the sparkly diamond fantasy of whatever it is and where those things come to me. I feel so lucky to be able to live in that dance, but also, I worked hard to cultivate that dance and figure out how we were going to dance.

Where do you think that combination came from?

That’s a great question.

Thank you.

Ha! I feel like you just go through life and try stuff and figure out what works for you the best. Maybe that was pretty evident when I was living in New York. I moved to LA from New York because I never saw the sky in New York and I have to see the sky…but that party I was at last night was really cool. I loved both but I didn’t know how to have both. How to have both to me was working in New York and then going to Oregon for two weeks in the summer and going camping…but also going to house parties and farms. Now I live those principles instead of borrowing from those principles. Now that’s what my life is built around.

And do you think that your tendency to go for the things you want allowed you to get both of those things?

Of course. Yeah, of course. And I want Mary to know that she can have that too. Whatever she wants. I want her to figure out how to… in some dark periods in the last year and a half I’ve been like, “I have to figure this out because I need my daughter to be proud of me and to know that she can do that too.” I just want her to be able to flourish. I don’t want her to just survive. I want her to thrive. And how is she going to get there? I need
to show her that it’s possible.
