So then I was always asking Joe, “can you please help me take a picture??” He’s always willing, of course. But I got into taking self-portraits because of the autonomy. So self-timer is my best friend, mainly with a Mamiya, most of the time. I mean, I still sprinkle in 35mm, even if it’s just disposable cameras. I always have one in my bag, but mostly Mamiya. How is it being married to another photographer? Oh, it’s cool. Joe is the kind of artist that won’t make something for a year and then he’ll go and make the most beautiful picture and I’m almost like, “fuck you. ” I have to be fully available and taking pictures all the time to keep that muscle alive and well and I feel like he can just turn it on and be like, “ah, I’m back.” But it’s great. We have a lot to talk about, photo-wise. We have the same interests, agriculture and photography, but I would say he’s more interested in agriculture than I am, and I’m more interested in photography than he is, it’s a nice balance. I love that he loves image-making and sometimes he makes these pictures that make me think, “oh my god, how did you even get that?” And he gets it so fast. I’ve been told I’m a pretty fast shooter by many people and I’m like, “you have not seen my husband.” The gut feeling, he is so good at just trusting that and coming out of this quiet time I had in my working life is a return to trusting in that gut feeling. He reminds me a lot that that’s my most important asset. Have your inspirations changed over the past few years? Yeah, I would say the list has gotten shorter. I’m looking to the ground a lot more because my kid’s down there. And I’m noticing bugs. And really, I have a macro lens now that I love. And I was like, “why did I never have a macro lens? This is so fun, seeing the world so small.” Sometimes I just use it for a portrait, but you can see the pores on the skin and I just…I used to be really interested in the landscape of the body and sensuality. And now I’m really interested in the landscape of the close-up, the close-up of my daughter’s eyes or my hair on her face or how the water drips off of her hair, small things like that. Details. Yeah, small details become the landscape. I was just so interested in the body in a landscape and the body becoming the landscape. And yeah, now it’s the details. It’s kind of the opposite of what Sally Mann talks about when her work, when she was shooting immediate family, and then she went into her landscape stuff, her children were still in the pictures, and then she kept zooming out. So it was way more the landscape than the pictures and than the children and the children disappeared all together, but I feel it’s the opposite for me. Maybe that’s because I became a mother much further into my photographic journey than she did. I also I had a very close friend of mine die, a year and a half ago now. And she respected all living beings down to like, the dung beetle, you know, and so I’ve been more appreciative of that, while we while she was here with us, but also after she died. Is there work you’re excited to make in the future? Oh, I mean always. I’m making a film. So that is very exciting. It might take a minute, but I’m making a film. A full length. You did a short about dog sled racing. Yeah, I did a short about about mushing, a short doc. I did my narrative short about the dancer, I’ve done plenty of music videos and things but definitely always craved doing something longer, so I’m excited about that. Is this one you’ve written yourself as well? Currently writing, yeah. It’s always about personal experiences, but made a little bit more palatable. How often are you taking pictures right now? I take a picture every day, sometimes that’s on my phone, and maybe it’s not something I’m going to put in a gallery, but it’s still using my visual brain. I go out to take pictures once a week, maybe twice a week. It depends on the weather, I get really inspired when it’s so lush and green outside and there’s rainbows and sometimes it’s raining and sometimes sunny and there’s flowers. You can be outside, not wearing a coat and you can sit on the ground. So, I’ll probably be taking more pictures now and then sometimes in the winter, less. Have you considered doing other shows, other books? For sure. I had a show last summer and books are how I think about pictures, it’s always a chapter of a book, but it’s such a thing to get them published. I think a book is warranted, but there’s nothing in the works right now. I’m always shooting for the next show and the next book so there there will be one. Do you see the chapters of your life clearly? Absolutely. In the pictures and the way I was taking pictures, oh yeah. How do you articulate those chapters to yourself? In a chapter of your life, what are the things you’re returning to? There are usually common themes, like, birds were really speaking to me then and I always wore this dress or whatever. It can seem like a superficial thing, but I think about it like, okay, if there’s a character in a movie that’s always wearing a red dress and suddenly she’s wearing a green dress, you think, okay, there’s something happening there and I feel like it’s the same in my life. It can come through clothing, it can come through a certain camera and how that makes you look at things a little differently. I get married to a camera for five years and then I move on. I don’t have to articulate it visually, it just happens, it’s not something I have to think about too hard. There are the common themes that I always come back to, you know, the body and the landscape, connection between people, pink, eggs, life and death, etc. When I think of your career, the chapters of your work, it feels very city-based for me, there’s the early Portland period, then there’s the New York period, then there’s the LA period and there’s the return to Oregon period. Totally, I think that’s accurate. The pictures that don’t resonate with me anymore are, yeah, the LA and New York pictures. I just like the pictures I’ve taken in Oregon. I like some of them, and I like certain projects I did. I think it’s more…maybe I just didn’t like my life as much. I liked the projects I would go shoot and seek out, but when I was documenting my everyday life, which is such a life force for me and my creativity. I mean, I had a nice life. I had a great life, but it wasn’t deeply inspiring to me. The professional work was inspiring. There’s a reason you came back to Oregon. It was a journey for you, where you had to have these other adventures to come back to Oregon. Absolutely. I think about it in terms of place as well, that’s an inherent change of scenery, and an indicator that something has changed because it’s very obvious something has changed! And there there is no anticipating what the next chapter is going to be? No, I can imagine, there’ll be more kids, we’ll definitely have one more. We might not stay in Oregon forever, we want to figure that out before Mary is school age. Where would you want to go? Probably Montana or Wyoming and have a more Western way of life. We don’t want to be chicken farming forever. Joe is a horse boy, he’s ridden horses his whole life. He’s a champion in endurance riding. We have his horse, we have my horse, but he doesn’t want to go trail ride anymore and we want to be working with animals. What we have here is wonderful, there are amazing people, it’s close to a lot of amenities. I’m not ready to leave, yet, but I imagine a world where we’re more in the wild. We want to be ranching rather than farming. Yeah, we’ve got a little time. But it goes by really quick, really quick. More horse photos is what you really want. Yeah! More horse photos. I always wanted to have an artist retreat when I lived in Eastern Oregon. That was kind of the plan, but then COVID hit and the place wasn’t really big enough for that. Maybe I could host a workshop or two, or a dinner, but we really want to have a dedicated place for artist retreats and also maybe a ranching school, because agriculture is dying in the US. It’s getting so much worse and young people can’t afford it, including us. You know, we have good other jobs and it’s so expensive. So thinking about something like that in the long term and also, I want a studio that’s separate from the house, we’re just thinking about things that would make a dream thing. And then also maybe some multi-generational living, probably closer to his family, because his parents are both retired and more available for helping with kids. It seems like you have a lot of ideas that seem possible to you, as grim as things can be. You have to think it’s possible or it won’t happen. Joe is a big dreamer and I’m a big dreamer who’s also a realist. We’ve had to meet each other in the middle, like, “okay, let’s dream, I can dream bigger but it also needs to be able to happen.” We’re crazy like that and also a good team, but I don’t think other people understand our decision-making, which is fine, only we need to understand our decision-making. It’s all seemed to really come together. It always does, maybe it takes a second, but it always does. Yeah, you’ve always seemed both aspirational and grounded. That’s the balance of living on a farm and working with my hands and also going to LA to go shoot Kesha or whatever it is. I need that sparkle, but also that rootedness and, honestly, that shit. I deal with poop every day. I need that, but also the sparkly diamond fantasy of whatever it is and where those things come to me. I feel so lucky to be able to live in that dance, but also, I worked hard to cultivate that dance and figure out how we were going to dance. Where do you think that combination came from? That’s a great question. Thank you. Ha! I feel like you just go through life and try stuff and figure out what works for you the best. Maybe that was pretty evident when I was living in New York. I moved to LA from New York because I never saw the sky in New York and I have to see the sky…but that party I was at last night was really cool. I loved both but I didn’t know how to have both. How to have both to me was working in New York and then going to Oregon for two weeks in the summer and going camping…but also going to house parties and farms. Now I live those principles instead of borrowing from those principles. Now that’s what my life is built around. And do you think that your tendency to go for the things you want allowed you to get both of those things? Of course. Yeah, of course. And I want Mary to know that she can have that too. Whatever she wants. I want her to figure out how to… in some dark periods in the last year and a half I’ve been like, “I have to figure this out because I need my daughter to be proud of me and to know that she can do that too.” I just want her to be able to flourish. I don’t want her to just survive. I want her to thrive. And how is she going to get there? I need to show her that it’s possible. Related

Entrevista 099 • 26 jul 2026

  • Entrevista de Lou Noble, Retratos de Olivia Bee por Joe Haeberle

Sobre Olivia Bee 2026

Olivia Bee es una fotógrafa y directora. Está intrigada por la magia de la vida cotidiana, la conexión inherente de un humano con la tierra, la dualidad del amor, y cómo la belleza de los recuerdos (real o imaginado) nos toca.

Se convirtió en la artista más joven en tener un libro publicado con la Fundación Aperture con la publicación de su monografía “Kids In Love” a los 22 años en 2016. La obra fue mostrada como una exposición individual en la Fundación Aperture, así como agnès b en la ciudad de Nueva York. Kioto ha sido incluida en exposiciones de grupo con Danziger Gallery, agnès b, Aperture Foundation, Weinstein Gallery, Bernal Espacio Galeria

Olivia ha dado dos charlas de Tedx y ha hablado en conferencias de todo el mundo. Ha estado lista en los directorios buscados de PDN 30 Under 30, y Forbes 30 Under 30.

Olivia vive en el suroeste de Oregon con su esposo, Joe y su hija, Mary. Ellos dirigen Y Knot Farm + Ranch en el valle Umpqua de Oregon, con un enfoque en carnes regenerativas y elevadas de pasto. El baile entre la raíz de la vida agrícola, y la chispa de los viajes internacionales, puntuada con la fabricación de arte, es lo que hace Olivia garrapata.

Enlaces

  • Sitio web »
  • Flickr »
  • Instagram »

Prefacio

Qué alegría, ver crecer y evolucionar a un fotógrafo. Hemos estado siguiendo el trabajo de Olivia Bee desde que empezó en Flickr. La entrevistamos por primera vez en 2014, cuando se constituyó en NY, y luego otra vez en 2018 cuando se mudó a Los Ángeles, y había planeado hacer que fuera un acontecimiento más regular... pero todos sabemos cómo fue 2022...

Tardó un rato, pero finalmente tuvimos que sentarnos con Olivia, ahora en Oregon, en otra fase de trabajo y vida. Todavía creando, todavía creciendo, todavía mucho ella misma.

-...
Esta entrevista ha sido editada para claridad y contenido.

Entrevista

Pasaremos enseguida. ¿Qué ha cambiado desde que te entrevistamos por última vez, hace ocho años?

¡Tanto! Ahora vivo en América rural, llevo una granja con mi esposo. Estoy casado. Tengo un hijo.

Me siento como si creciera en la ciudad sin saber que algunas cosas eran una opción. Nunca supe que podrías vivir en América rural o que podrías tener un caballo. Sólo pensé que era algo en lo que naciste y que no podías elegir eso. Pero, ya sabes, siempre había inklings de este tipo de cosas cuando era un niño pequeño. Siempre estábamos jardinero y mis padres tenían un gran patio.

Sí, lo más importante, sin embargo, ¿cómo va el trabajo? Los bebés son agradables y todo, pero ¿qué hay de la fotografía!

Es bueno! Sólo quiero hacer la infancia más mágica para mi hija. Y así que eso termina siendo en fotos porque siempre estoy fotografiando lo que estoy pasando en mi vida y lo que está pasando, ya sea una circunstancia externa o observación o un monólogo interno o fantasía. He estado fotografiando nuestra vida en la granja, pero con esta nueva inclinación mágica. Estoy siendo dibujado para hacer disfraces y hacer pequeñas casas fueraapier-mâché, creciendo como una tonelada de flores para que mi hija pueda estar en un campo de flores. Mi vida viene primero, mis fotografías vienen segundo, pero mis fotografías son siempre evidencia de esa vida, o prueba. Viene de la vida primero y siempre ha sido así. Así que es bueno. Estoy filmando más trabajo comercial, que es realmente divertido. Me siento como lo necesito. Es generativo para mí para salir y ser un viaje creativo

¿Cómo se siente el campo profesional por ti? Los últimos años han sido muy tumultuosos para las personas en fotografía.

Hay mucho que temer. Y trato de no ir allí, porque entonces no puedo salir. Con AI, ya sabes, algunas carreras de gente acaban, si no pivotes, se va a ir. Hay este empuje, el mundo va en dos direcciones diferentes en términos de visuales, hay el súper-obvioso, "perfecto AI puede hacer esto

Es parte del ecosistema.

Sí, exactamente. No están pensando en eso. Están pensando en cortar sus números, no como, ¿dónde va a estar nuestro consumidor? Y ves a la gente que lucha, es decir, obviamente, gas ahora mismo. Sólo hacer la vida es mucho más caro de lo que solía ser. Pero la gente parece ser pagada menos, a través de la junta, no sólo en la industria de la fotografía, creo que en general, no aumenta aún sus impuestos suben, el gas es más caro
son más, sólo todo es más caro. Todo lo que decir, estoy eligiendo ser optimista. Y que la gente siempre querrá un toque humano. Y siento que siempre va a haber doom y gloom. Es bastante tenso.

En nuestra industria, siempre puedes ser como, “bueno, no era como los años 80. Bueno, no era como los primeros años 2000”. Y así que intento pensar en términos de, bien, qué en 20 años la gente va a ser como, “Dios, ojalá pudiera volver a eso. No era como si fuera en 2026.” Lo cual suena loco decir en voz alta, pero ¿cuáles son las vías para desarrollarse y tratar de

Parte de eso también, me rodea con gente positiva. Personas que reconocen las dificultades en la industria, pero quieren seguir adelante y desear
La gente siempre va a necesitar un toque humano, la gente siempre va a querer historias humanas, o al menos el mundo en el que quiero vivir y el mundo que quiero para mi hija. Y aunque ese mundo sea quizás menos que el mundo entero, creo que todavía va a estar allí.

¿Te sientes como si tuvieras un equilibrio ahora mismo entre como tu arte y tu vida?

Siento que tengo un equilibrio entre mi arte y mi vida, pero es un baile siempre cambiante, especialmente con la estacionalidad del trabajo agrícola. Admito, no estoy haciendo tanto del trabajo manual como solía hacer porque soy el cuidador principal y Joe tiene que estar en el tractor mucho, pero me siento tan afortunado por María, también, porque ambos somos capaces de estar en casa. 24-7 Ella tiene que estar con nosotros.

Cuando eres madre te has convertido en un poco más eficiente con tu tiempo o tal vez ineficiente de otras maneras, pero como, “de acuerdo tengo 15 minutos mientras ella está jugando con bloques o dormido o está realmente en este libro, mejor aprovechar este 15 minutos porque voy a querer estar con ella
después de que ella no está enfocada en algo más o si ella no está durmiendo.” Es un desafío. Las cosas comerciales no suelen estar en el horario. Mi agenda se basa en su horario y luego espero que otras cosas encajan en él o tengo que averiguarlo. Me gustaría estar trabajando más, me encantaría estar haciendo un tiro al mes, creo que me voy a volver a eso. Todo es como se supone que es hermoso.

Solía ser como, “Ojalá pudiera hacer mi trabajo personal y no hacer ningún trabajo comercial.” Y lo hice. Y realmente apesta ser un artista hambriento. Es una mierda. No era creativo, porque estaba en modo de supervivencia, y sé que mucha gente puede relacionarse con eso. Estaba literalmente pensando, “¿cómo vamos a hacer estos próximos pagos de factura?” No estoy pensando, “oh, se convirtió en una forma de trabajar”

¿Por qué crees que tu carrera ha sobrevivido cuando otras personas parecen estar desatando?

No creo que haya venido sin flagelación, definitivamente he tenido momentos de flagelación o de pensar, ¿es este flagelaje? o, “la inundación viene”. Definitivamente tengo suerte, de alguna manera. Siempre estoy tratando de... sí, tomaré un millón de fotos de mí mismo en un campo al atardecer, pero estoy tratando de hacer cosas nuevas, también.

No trato de seguir las tendencias. Trato de averiguar qué es lo siguiente para mí y qué es interesante para mí y espero que eso cambie. Me di cuenta después Kids in Love Y después de mudarme a América rural, “de acuerdo, no puedo ser contratado para niños que se divierten en el mundo para siempre, porque no voy a ser un niño en el mundo que se divierta para siempre.” Miro a Rihanna, ella ha evolucionado tantas veces. Y ella hace cosas en su propia línea de tiempo. Siempre estoy pensando, “bien, ¿qué haría Rihannaically? Ella probablemente se haría algo diferente.

¿Sigues usando formato grande ahora mismo?

No realmente. Es demasiado caro. Estoy seguro de que volveré a él. También estaba ansioso por algo entre formato grande y 35 mm, así que he estado filmando sobre todo formato medio y tratando de casarse con esos dos mundos. Quería una manera más rápida de hacer imágenes. Tenía un auto-tiempo que había hecho esta compañía robótica para tomar fotos con mi gran autonomía de formato ... pero no duraron siempre que preguntar.

¿Cómo es estar casado con otro fotógrafo?

Oh, es genial. Joe es el tipo de artista que no hará algo por un año y luego va a ir y hacer la imagen más hermosa y yo soy
casi como, "te jodas". Tengo que estar completamente disponible y tomar fotos todo el tiempo para mantener ese músculo vivo y bien y siento que él puede simplemente encenderlo y ser como, "ah, estoy de vuelta." Pero es genial. Tenemos mucho de qué hablar, foto-sólo. Tenemos los mismos intereses, agricultura y fotografía,
pero diría que está más interesado en la agricultura que yo, y estoy más interesado en la fotografía que él, es un buen equilibrio.

Me encanta que le encanta la creación de imágenes y a veces hace estas fotos que me hacen pensar, “oh dios mío, ¿cómo lo conseguiste?” Y él lo consigue tan rápido. Me han dicho que soy un shooter bastante rápido por muchas personas y soy como, “no has visto a mi marido.” El sentimiento de tripa, él es tan bueno sólo confiar en eso y salir de este tiempo tranquilo que tuve en mi vida de trabajo es un retorno a confiar en él

¿Han cambiado tus inspiraciones en los últimos años?

Sí, yo diría que la lista se ha hecho más corta. Estoy mirando al suelo mucho más porque mi hijo está ahí abajo. Y estoy notando errores. Y realmente, tengo una lente macro ahora que me encanta. Y yo era como, "¿por qué nunca tuve una lente macro? Esto es tan divertido, viendo el mundo tan pequeño . A veces sólo lo uso para un retrato, pero usted puede ver los poros de la piel cerca de la piel
cómo el agua se gotea de su pelo, cosas pequeñas como esas.

Detalles.

Sí, los detalles pequeños se convierten en el paisaje. Estaba tan interesado en el cuerpo en un paisaje y el cuerpo convirtiéndose en el paisaje. Y sí, ahora son los detalles. Es como el opuesto de lo que Sally Mann habla cuando su trabajo, cuando ella estaba disparando a la familia inmediata, y luego ella entró en sus cosas de paisaje, sus hijos todavía estaban en las fotos, y luego ella siguió ampliando. Así que era mucho más el paisaje que los niños desaparecidos

Yo también tuve una amiga muy cercana de mi muerte, hace un año y medio. Y ella respetaba a todos los seres vivientes a gusto, el escarabajo estiércol estiércol, ya sabes, y así he sido más apreciativo de eso, mientras que nosotros mientras ella estaba aquí con nosotros, pero también después de su muerte.

¿Hay trabajo que estás emocionado de hacer en el futuro?

Quiero decir, siempre. Estoy haciendo una película. Así que eso es muy emocionante. Podría tomar un minuto, pero estoy haciendo una película. Una longitud completa.

Hiciste un cortocircuito sobre carreras de trineo de perros.

Sí, hice un corto acerca de la mushing, un corto doc. Hice mi narrativa corta sobre la bailarina, he hecho un montón de vídeos de música y cosas, pero definitivamente siempre anhelado hacer algo más, así que estoy emocionado por eso.

¿Es éste el que te has escrito también?

Actualmente escribiendo, sí. Siempre se trata de experiencias personales, pero se hace un poco más agradable.

¿Con qué frecuencia tomas fotos ahora mismo?

Tomo una foto todos los días, a veces eso está en mi teléfono, y tal vez no es algo que voy a poner en una galería, pero todavía está usando mi cerebro visual. Salgo a tomar fotos una vez a la semana, tal vez dos veces a la semana. Depende del tiempo, me siento realmente inspirado cuando es tan exuberante y verde exterior y hay arco iris y a veces está lloviendo y a veces es más soleado y hay flores fuera.

¿Has considerado hacer otros shows, otros libros?

Por supuesto. Tuve un show el verano pasado y los libros son cómo pienso en las imágenes, siempre es un capítulo de un libro, pero es algo así para publicarlas. Creo que un libro está justificado, pero no hay nada en los trabajos ahora mismo. Siempre estoy filmando para el próximo show y el próximo libro para que allí va a haber uno.

¿Ves claramente los capítulos de tu vida?

Por supuesto, en las fotos y en la forma en que tomaba fotos, oh sí.

¿Cómo se articulan esos capítulos a sí mismo?

En un capítulo de tu vida, ¿cuáles son las cosas a las que estás volviendo? Normalmente hay temas comunes, como, los pájaros realmente me hablaban entonces y siempre usé este vestido o lo que sea. Puede parecer algo superficial, pero pienso en ello como, vale, si hay un personaje en una película que siempre lleva un vestido rojo y de repente ella está usando un vestido verde, piensas, está bien, hay algo que sucede allí y yo también creo que

Cuando pienso en tu carrera, los capítulos de tu trabajo, se siente muy basado en la ciudad para mí, hay el período temprano de Portland, entonces hay el período de Nueva York, entonces hay el período de Los Ángeles y hay el regreso a Oregon período.

Totalmente, creo que eso es exacto. Las fotos que no resonan conmigo son, sí, las imágenes de Los Ángeles y Nueva York. Me gusta las fotos que he tomado en Oregon. Me gustan algunos de ellos, y me gustan ciertos proyectos que hice. Creo que es más...quizás no me gustó tanto mi vida. Me gustó los proyectos que me gustó mucho.
iría disparando y buscando, pero cuando estaba documentando mi vida cotidiana, que es una fuerza de vida para mí y mi creatividad. Quiero decir, tuve una vida agradable. Tuve una gran vida, pero no fue profundamente inspirador para mí. El trabajo profesional fue inspirador.

Hay una razón por la que regresaste a Oregon. Fue un viaje para ti, donde tenías que tener estas otras aventuras para volver a Oregon.

Absolutamente. Pienso en ello también en términos de lugar, que es un cambio inherente del paisaje, y un indicador que algo ha cambiado porque es muy obvio que algo ha cambiado!

¿Y no hay ninguna anticipación de lo que va a ser el próximo capítulo?

No, puedo imaginar, habrá más niños, definitivamente tendremos uno más. No podemos quedarnos en Oregon para siempre, queremos averiguarlo antes de que María sea la edad escolar.

¿A dónde quieres ir?

Probablemente Montana o Wyoming y tener una forma más occidental de vida. No queremos ser pollos para siempre. Joe es un niño de caballo, él es caballos montados toda su vida. Él es un campeón en la carrera de resistencia. Tenemos su caballo, tenemos mi caballo, pero él no quiere ir de paseo por el sendero y queremos estar trabajando con animales.

Lo que tenemos aquí es maravilloso, hay gente increíble, está cerca de muchas comodidades. No estoy listo para salir, sin embargo, pero me imagino un mundo donde estamos más en el salvaje. Queremos ser ganaderos en lugar de cultivar. Sí, tenemos un poco de tiempo. Pero va por muy rápido, realmente rápido.

Más fotos de caballos es lo que realmente quieres.

Si! Más fotos de caballos. Siempre quise tener un retiro de artista cuando vivía en Oregón Oriental. Eso fue algo así, pero luego COVID golpeó y el lugar no era lo suficientemente grande para eso. Tal vez podría albergar un taller o dos, o una cena, pero realmente queremos tener un lugar dedicado para retiros de artistas y también quizás una escuela de ranchería, porque la agricultura está muriendo en los Estados Unidos. Se está volviendo mucho peor y los jóvenes pueden

Así que pensando en algo así a largo plazo y también, quiero un estudio que está separado de la casa, estamos pensando en cosas que harían algo de sueño. Y entonces también tal vez una vida multigeneracional, probablemente más cerca de su familia, porque sus padres están tanto jubilados como más disponibles para ayudar con los niños.

Parece que tienes muchas ideas que parecen posibles para ti, lo más sombrío que pueden ser las cosas.

Tienes que pensar que es posible o no sucederá. Joe es un gran soñador y soy un gran soñador que también es un realista. Foreword

Photography, real photography, is about loss. The face across a decade. The motel sign on a county road in New Mexico that will be a foundation slab and some weeds in five years. Everything you love, forgotten. Most photographers photograph this and call it nostalgia. Ben Fraternale photographs it like a man trying to outrun his own demise.

He's thirty-three. He lives in New York. He has built a career on a film stock that's been niche since he was in high school, and he wants, in his own words, to take your funeral photo. The good kind. The one that gets you remembered.
-Agustin Sanchez

Interview

When you’re taking pictures right now, what is it you’re trying to do?

It’s a constantly evolving thing.  One day I’m a preservationist, another day I’m just taking pictures of people and deriving joy out of that, but I think, ultimately, I’m driven by a need to instill moments and images in time, and something about that is core to my person. How that manifests in the images themselves is not necessarily so vividly clear to me, but I’m always trying to steal a moment, in particular when I’m on the road and I’m traveling, which, I travel a lot, so it’s become very core to my photography.

I love endlessly searching and adventuring and driving for hours, looking for things I sometimes never find, but when I find that thing, if I can capture that moment in time and make it something timeless, I think that’s what I’m looking for.

And it manifests in a variety of ways. I think with Polaroid, it’s the perfect format for doing that because you create something physical out of reality in an instant. You end up with this physical object of a place, especially with the Polaroid 8×10 format. That’s part of why I love that format maybe the most, because it’s the ultimate example of this. It’s the closest “stealing” of a moment that you can get. That’s my vibe right now, although it’s always changing.

When you’re making the Route 66 images and looking at old motels, do you know what it is you’re looking for when you see it?

Yes, I really do. There is a fine line in my journeys,, between something that’s decrepit and makes me feel sad, and something that looks like someone has put care into maintaining some sort of visual presence, an aesthetic that actually is preserving that place.

I’m occasionally drawn to something that’s dilapidated or has a particularly interesting condition. But I think, for the most part, when I see a motel that looks plucked out of the 50s, I’m like, okay, my photo of that thing may also look plucked out of the 50s or have 50s vibe modern spin on it.

I think a lot of people who shoot the kinds of subjects that I shoot often end up depicting the imagery in a way that makes me dour, because you feel the loss that has come from time. And I’m more trying to celebrate time itself and not necessarily show something in its worst state.

What is it you want someone to take from a photo of one of those motels? What do you want your audience to feel?

I want them to feel like they’re looking at a postcard they found in a drawer that has some handwriting on the back. I want someone to feel transported. That’s the main thing for me,  whether it’s because it’s particularly alluring or because there are elements in the light and color that draw them in, I want them to feel like, “oh wow, I’m standing there.” Especially because the Polaroid format brings unreality into the mix, but have it still feel like this is an artifact of something. Like when you go into a museum and you look at an old image, it brings you there for a moment.

There’s that one big Polaroid you took of, you know, the Manhattan skyline. What is it you want someone to take from that? Because that’s slightly different than trying to preserve a feeling.

It is, it is different. That image in particular was interesting…I grew up in Manhattan. And my memory of going to the top of buildings and overlooking things is colored with a bit of the stuff that your memory sprinkles onto images. And getting the opportunity to even be in the position to take that photo was very fortunate. And I felt, because I had that opportunity, I wanted to make something that had an almost dream-like, almost gothic, heightened look to it. That’s what I was pulling from in my own memory because I could have taken that picture 10 minutes later, it would have looked completely different. 10 minutes earlier, would have looked completely different. I took the photo in that moment because that was the feeling I got  in that moment of the light and the way the buildings looked.

One thing I don’t know if I’ve heard before is how you got into Polaroid specifically?

Well, Polaroid has been around me so much and I’ve used it so much over my lifetime, through elementary school, into high school. It being a thing that I would bring to the last day of school or, you know, it was an accessory that my mom basically would put in my hands and say, “now go to school” and/or “now go see a friend.”

“I want lunch.”

“No son, no lunch, but I did buy you this 10-pack of film.” Growing up around it,  and having handled it so much growing up, I grew to associate it with a lot of things and a lot of key moments in my life. As I grew as a photographer and entered the professional field, I entered a malaise that a lot of people are familiar with, where you’re using digital tools so much in your professional life, and you use those same tools in your personal work, you start to lose some sort of connection. You think, “what am I actually doing? Is this enjoyable? What am I missing here?”  Then my mom reintroduced me to it, she got me an Instax Mini right in the early Impossible era, and I fell in love with it again.

I was using it solely as a party thing, it took me a few years to realize it might be the missing piece. There is something that I was looking for that I wasn’t getting out of pointing a sensor at a person or an object ,that I began getting from the magic of a Polaroid, and that switch flipped immediately. It was not a gradual thing, it was like, “okay, this is related to my past, this is related to my future, this is something I’m connecting with on a tactile level,” and I think it just clicked. From then on, pretty much, it’s been a daily driver.

Do you remember when that was?

I think that was probably 2016. That was when I started. And the photos from that time are still not particularly artistic, or don’t necessarily match up to what I’m doing now, but they were the early stages of starting to understand this feeling. And it took years for it to grow. Probably seven years ago is when I really snapped into it and started seeking things that I thought would be perfect for Polaroid.

Why do you think that change happened?

I mean, this is such a bad answer, but this is the honest truth. I had been shooting Canon digital cameras forever. And I got a Panasonic GH4 for video production. And as a result of that, switching over systems, I started using it as a photo camera. That basically deleted my interest in photography. I literally stopped taking photos and I didn’t even consciously realize why it had happened. In picking up the Polaroid again, and starting to apply it, that’s when the switch flipped. I had totally lost this thing, and it came surging back. From then on I was completely Polaroid-pilled.

When you look at kind of those early Polaroids, do you understand what that
evolution was for yourself?

It was so abrupt in some ways that I feel like I immediately was seeking what I’m still seeking today. So the evolution has been more in methodology than what I actually was seeking through Polaroid. I’m getting the same thing that I got from it, you know, in 2018 or whatever that was. How I’m going about it has changed, my techniques have changed. But the actual core driver is basically the same. I’m 33 years old, turning 34 shortly, and I’ve gone through many periods of my life with obsessive interest in certain things. I really am obsessive about the things that I love.

Cocaine/photographs/traveling.

Exactly. But this started as something where I was wondering, “is this a phase? Is this something that is scratching an itch right now that is eventually going to sort of fade a little bit?” But it didn’t. It only grew. It grew even more when I started meeting people that were associated with the product’s creation, other people who use it, finding that community element, and finding an audience as well, people who want to even look at my images, and that are interested in techniques and how I did certain things. It all fed in together.

 

How has your work changed since becoming popular in the Polaroid community?

It’s encouraged me to push myself. I think I’m very self-competitive, very self versus self. I’m constantly trying to improve and seek the next great thing that I can do. Having community, having people that react to things that I’m doing live, it helps keep me honest about all those things and keeps me more focused, because it’s arbitrary. It’s not commercial mainstream popularity. It’s all something on an app or someone in a comment section or friends, but it’s still a motivator and still a guide for me to think, “okay, I can’t not post for the next two months. I’m a professional freelancer. You constantly need a kick in the butt.

Yes, to a degree. China was an interesting one because I was limited in what I actually chose to do. I was essentially guided through the experience.

How did the China trip come about?

But this man sent me an email, told me he was a big fan of my YouTube channel, felt like we were kindred spirits,  that we needed to immediately start talking about Polaroid, we need to start chatting. And if the mood strikes, I’m invited to Shanghai whenever I want, he can show me the city, we can make it an In An Instant episode. He basically just threw it all out there, wrote the email, and I just couldn’t let it go. The thought of doing that was so interesting to me. As someone who’s always seeking, I was like, “well, this is an interesting thing to go out and do and an adventure that could change my life.”

A few months pass, I get my visa, and I go out there. I met probably a hundred different people, I was constantly being introduced to artists, to people in the government, constantly going to interesting places and completely foreign places.. I had never been in Asia, so it was a true culture shock. And I find that culture shock is difficult to experience these days because of our exposure to literally everything that’s ever happened. It was an actual genuine experience that was surprising in every corner.

And to your earlier question, on day two, we got back to our hoteland we’re like, “what are we doing here? What exactly are we trying to show here? Did we, in those first two days,  actually do anything that would provide value to people, or did we just  nod our heads and go along with the next thing that was happening?” And from that point on, we started pushing more against something we were being presented or, for example, we were introduced to a bunch of cosplayers and someone was taking their photos and the guy I was with was like, “here, you can take the photos of the cosplayers as well. You definitely should jump in there and do that.” And I was thinking about it, that’s not really my thing, I stepped away. A few minutes later we circled back to it and I was like, “I gotta be honest. I’m more interested in the human beings that I can more easily relate to and potentially are more interesting because they are authentically themselves in this moment, versus someone who is portraying a character or essentially modeling.”

I was much more interested in photographing the photographer, this crazy guy who brought five boxes of Polaroid 8×10 film on a Wednesday to this shoot. Once I peeled that layer back, I got to have this unbelievable relationship with this guy, Leo, who was the one shooting the cosplayers in the first place. I kept pushing us to fight against shooting pure artifice and try to get something a little bit more humanistic. Ultimately that was the most important thing to me, both in the images and the video. And I think it’s something we actually  accomplished, which under that level of stress and moving as quickly as we were, I think that’s an interesting accomplishment. I’m pretty proud of that.

When you guys are were the Great Wall of China, you definitely seemed to have a strong idea of what you wanted to capture. What did you want from those pictures?

That’s a good example…as we were all on the train going to the Great Wall, we were discussing it. What do we want to do there? We’re going to be under pressure. Security is going to be coming after us. This is unsanctioned, to a degree, and we just need to go out there and do it. And under that strain, it’s difficult to think, “how do I want to organize a frame? What am I exactly trying to show here?” But I was interested in taking the Polaroid frame and creating a standalone object that is aesthetically interesting and well-organized. Something that you could put on a wall as a memento of the Great Wall of China.

Whether or not we captured it on that day is in question, because it was very difficult and we lost several frames because we were trying to process the film at the Great Wall. But in a lot of these instances where you’re in this completely foreign place that has been photographed a bajillion times, one of the most critical elements to me is, maybe it’s been done a billion times, but they’re not me standing here with film that’s been expired for 20 years, where no one knows exactly what it’s going to look like.

No one is going to be able to create this image other than me right now. And that’s part of the magic to me of Polaroid, you’ve got this alchemy of a person taking the photo plus this image that is also a living, breathing one-of-a-kind object. That’s what gets me excited about shooting even the most  generic thing. And I think I brought home stuff that’s…at least it’s my stuff, even if it’s been done, you know, by tourists over generations.

So for you, the tools that you use provide a lot of your voice.

I would say so. I am easily overwhelmed by the notion of that idea, of every subject being shot before and that everyone’s seen everything before. But creating something that has a unique imprint is doable in a billion ways. As photographers, we know this, you can manipulate light, you can manipulate your subject. But for me, when you’re shooting something that’s kind of an objective scene, such as the Great Wall of China, it’s not going to pose for you.

You have to take your tools and make something that is at least somewhat unique to you that, in many ways, is tied to the format itself. When there’s human beings involved, you’ve got a little bit of a different equation. And we did a lot of portraiture out there. But again, they were under these interesting conditions where you can’t really communicate well with the person you’re shooting. You can only move them so much. In some cases, we were shooting people that were nearing 100 years-old.

They are fragile! They might break!

Yeah, they might break. Just as delicate as the camera. In those cases, I’m leaning into the format itself as my mode of expression, because I feel that it lends a uniqueness to whatever you’re doing. If you’re taking a photo of this 95 year-old cherished artist, he’s never been shot like this before, you know, even if it’s even if it’s a resting expression portrait, it still has captured his soul in a way that’s unique in the modern day. The tools and myself go very hand in hand. We hold hands skipping down the beach.

When you were studying film and photography in school, are there photographers who are touchstones in your mind when you’re making art?

I don’t use photographers as a guide. Because my origins were more filmmaking-based, you know, I learned on Tarantino and Christopher Nolan and Stanley Kubrick and a lot of David Lynch, a lot of core filmmakers drove my early interest in making visual art. So when my photography branched from video, I didn’t necessarily gain new inspiration. A lot of what drove me originally and what I thought would become my main canvas was depicting cinematic scenes with photography. That was what I was originally interested in doing. And to a degree, I do find Route 66, mid-century America, very cinematic. When you just look at the film Paris, Texas, you can map some of my photos onto that film. You know, I love Stephen Shore as much as the next guy, but I don’t necessarily look at his images and think I gotta go get out there right now. I more look at my own images and think, oh, I gotta get out there right now and make something that is more true to me or is better than the last thing.

Do you have people that inspire you, now?

I would say, someone like Fred Johnson, who is a Polaroid guy, he makes these miniatures of himself and puts them into miniature scenes. And while that is completely different than the type of thing that I would do, I love the way he’s baking reality into unreality. That is something that I try at least once a month, as part of the 1212 project, because it’s an excuse to experiment. And so that, his style, the kinds of things he’s doing, it’s inspiring, especially through Polaroid, which adds this additional layer of almost confusion, when you’re looking at a scene that is real, but something is off a little bit, the chemistry is melting that all together.

I’m obsessed with Jamie Swick and her work. I find myself in nature very often as a result of being in these unusual places. And her work and her ability to create emotion out of a tree, or  ind the color in something that I wouldn’t normally look closely at, she encourages me to be much more observant.

Honestly, and this is aspirational, but Walter Iooss. He’s one of the greatest sports photographers of all times and he’s taken some of the most unbelievable images of athletes that I’ve ever seen. He’s a constant inspiration to me. Ironically, I work with athletes almost every day, shooting video, but the photo element only comes in now and again. And so that’s sort of an aspirational one where I look at him and it pushes me to want to go out and do that. And figure out, how am I gonna do that? That’s something I want to do more of going forward, because it really is the marriage of my two biggest interests.

How has your YouTube project, In An Instant, influenced your photography?

I don’t think it has had a direct impact on the images that I make. More it’s given me the opportunity to explore what goes into the images with much more depth, and has given me a layer of consciousness that I didn’t have before, where every time I publish something, I’m thinking about the layers of it, how it’s perceived, how I created it, what tools were used to make it, what I meant to do when I made it. It gets me excited to make work, it’s another motivator, because it’s like, all right, we’re making a video about the SX-70 right now. I have a thousand photos I’ve taken with it in the past, but I’d rather go out right now and take a thousand more. Right now I’m testing a new SX-70 modification. I’ve used the SX-70 a thousand times, but it’s making me very stoked to go out the door and go find something. In An Instant gives me these excuses to do that with my everyday life. And as a freelancer, thankfully, I have pockets of time to explore that.

What’s your favorite photo that you’ve taken?

I mean, the Manhattan skyline photo is an interesting one because it does feel so fundamental to me. It feels like a bio photo or like if I died, they would show it. Alongside that, I also have a couple of 8×10 images of my grandfather that are particularly special. He was an artist, he was a hand illustrator, he was an actor, and I was following all these levels of his life when I was growing up, and then to end up…he’s 93 years old. I’m taking his 8×10 right now. That just felt like sort of this natural photo that had to be made, and so to have done that with him was really special, and so that photo is particularly core to me.

There’s another recent one, which was just my wife’s house at Christmas time, doing a long exposure of the family with the tree. Again, it felt like a personal memory that I’m going to look back on in 50 years and be able to just be standing right there. The camera and that process helps me ground myself in those moments and helps me place myself in time, as well. I’m really overactive and I really do so much. Everything can start blurring together, but when I look at one of those images I’m like, okay, I remember what it smelled like, I remember what my feet felt like standing there, so those three I think immediately come to mind. They also happen to be directly in front of me.

Top three photos I can see. What is it about the 8×10 versus, you know, a regular Polaroid, you know, or a 4×5?

I think the 8×10 is, first of all, it’s a more unique and true replication of a person or a place because of the field of view and because of what the lensing is doing. It’s a more natural POV than light coming through a cone and then going into a very small place. It’s giving you this more natural scale replica of reality, which in the end I think is one of the core things that I’m after. And then there’s also this intimacy that happens when you’re shooting either a person or a place. The amount of time you’re standing there and considering things and making the tiniest little movements and changes of focus.

Those all just make it a more interesting experience to me and I think the images are always reflective of that because you feel like you can’t blow it if you if you throw up an 8×10, like, it screws up your day and maybe even your life. So it puts this extra onus on the actual process of it that you get that feeling with a typical Polaroid picture because it is so special. But I think it’s different with 8×10 and it just hits different than when you’re holding a 4×5. It’s still this small thing. With the 8×10 the fact that you can hold it and you’re just like, bam, that is in your face.

It’s such a special experience, especially when you’re doing it with someone else. You get this core moment where you’re both looking at this object and you’re just like. “wow, how is this even possible?” Those moments are so hard to come by. We’re in this ridiculous time and actually having a moment of genuine “whoa”. I’m always chasing that.

When you are photographing someone, is it helpful having that laborious process? How does that affect what you’re going for with a portrait?

As someone with the cinematography background, the feeling of setting up the lights carefully orchestrating the environment that you’re in, you’re not necessarily just being like, “hey, can you stand there? Boom.” You’re organizing the environment, the light, and the person. It’s more romantic for everyone involved.

It helps bring whatever I’m trying to bring out of that person because they feel like they’re in a movie almost, they feel like they’re in the 1800s with this gigantic camera and they want to be involved and give you something that you haven’t gone before. It can be hard to make someone feel comfortable in that circumstance. I’ve definitely encountered people who are like, “I’m like standing still for a minute. Do you have a sense of what it is you want from a subject when you’re trying to take a portrait?

Yeah, I’m just trying to bring out the core beauty of somebody, show them in…I want to take the funeral photo. I want to take the beautiful, stately picture of somebody on this large format that represents them like no other and give them an art object of themselves. I think that’s what I’m looking for more than, “oh, she’s really happy. She should be smiling.” I am trying to bring something out of someone that might not necessarily be the most basic thing. Subtly and with light and with lens and with their eyes and all of those elements.

Just through the process of taking photos every day and trying to capture whatever the keystone moment is of this day or this trip or this time. Yeah, it was kind of horrifying. And it was kind of scary. There’s no record of…

What was scary about it?

It was scary to not have any record of existence and not have…I am very nostalgia-obsessed, and by that I mean, I like staring at something and feeling what it felt like to be there and think of all the elements that went into the moment and not being able to have access to any of that was scary because, you know, my memory is however good it is, but it’s, it’s not as good as a picture and it’s not as good as being able to travel through a picture into your mind palace and place yourself in that moment. And I was scared by the lack of any record of any of it.

What is it that draws you to that feeling of nostalgia?

I think about this all the time. That phrase, “nostalgia is a drug,” I actually feel like a chemical thing when I’m going through time in my mind. And I’ve always been chasing that feeling. It’s like, I’m trying to actually put it into words. It’s hard to put into words. But I remember when my Aunt Kibbe was dying, she was like 99 years-old, and I was thinking, “this is going to be inaccessible in my mind, this space, this time, if I don’t do something about it.”

Or when I was moving out of college and I was thinking, “this apartment is insane, it’s a piece of shit. But if I don’t do something about that and start filming it or take photos of it, then I’ll have no way to reflect back on this.” And I do honestly think it has to do with this thought I had growing up of, “what is our place in the world? What is the impermanence of humanity? We are so irrelevant in the grand scheme of things, so we have to create some sort of trail for ourselves. Otherwise, none of this matters.” And I do think that that has very much..that’s just in my blood. Nostalgia is connected to that. Being able to access the past, knowing that it’s gone, is a superpower.

I mean, to you, it feels like if you don’t record it, you’ll lose it.

Yeah, 100%. 100%, I do feel like it’s lost. And I don’t trust my own memory to have the detailed… I don’t trust my own memory and I don’t trust my own process of being alive to be able to encase life itself without that. And now I don’t fear it anymore because I obsessively do it. But I think when you see people shooting endlessly on iPhones or photos going to cloud storage, I think almost the same thing is happening. Yes, you can sit there and scroll through your phone, but you will lose that. That will go away. Whether or not that’s now or in 200 years, no one’s going to open up a cardboard box and find your old clothes and your phone in there and wake up your cloud library. It’s just not going to happen. And so making these physical objects, especially through Polaroid, is that immediate moment of creation and installation and piece of nostalgia you can hold forever until it fades away. But, you know, everything will fade away eventually.

I mean…you just fear death. Let’s just get it out there!

Well yeah! What’s funny is, I didn’t fear death growing up. I was very emboldened for some reason. I was very aware of death and that it was going to come and I think it’s not necessarily fear of dying, it’s a fear of dying and nothing’s there when you’re dead, oblivion, there’s no Ben anymore after he dies, but there may be this register of his life that, if someone bothers to, they can go through and access it.

And I think that is weirdly intangible for many people, and I am creating something tangible so that it doesn’t happen to me.

It’s not death, it’s being forgotten. It’s that if you’re not remembered, it doesn’t matter.

Yeah, if you’re not remembered and if there’s no trail, if there’s no trace, that is scary to me. I think that this all ties into the stuff that I like shooting, because when I’m out on Route 66 or I’m out in the middle of America and I’m out in these random places that even the most well-drawn collector of old sites has seen, I do feel like the Polaroid and this process is doing that thing. It’s taking the world that is disappearing and is constantly changing and that we’ll have no trace of and it’s making a physical thing of it.

And same with a portrait of a person. When I say I want to take the funeral photo, that’s what I’m talking about. Taking this image that is emblematic and can be looked back on and it leaves a trace and it leaves a record. And it’s a classical concept. It’s something that was basically started with the very first realistic paintings, but that is the kind of thing I’m after. It’s the encapsulation.

It’s a constantly evolving thing. One day I’m a preservationist, another day I’m just taking pictures of people and deriving joy out of that, but I think, ultimately, I’m driven by a need to instill moments and images in time, and something about that is core to my person. How that manifests in the images themselves is not necessarily so vividly clear to me, but I’m always trying to steal a moment, in particular when I’m on the road and I’m traveling, which, I travel a lot, so it’s become very core to my photography.
