And it manifests in a variety of ways. I think with Polaroid, it’s the perfect format for doing that because you create something physical out of reality in an instant. You end up with this physical object of a place, especially with the Polaroid 8×10 format. That’s part of why I love that format maybe the most, because it’s the ultimate example of this. It’s the closest “stealing” of a moment that you can get. That’s my vibe right now, although it’s always changing. When you’re making the Route 66 images and looking at old motels, do you know what it is you’re looking for when you see it? Yes, I really do. There is a fine line in my journeys,, between something that’s decrepit and makes me feel sad, and something that looks like someone has put care into maintaining some sort of visual presence, an aesthetic that actually is preserving that place. I’m occasionally drawn to something that’s dilapidated or has a particularly interesting condition. But I think, for the most part, when I see a motel that looks plucked out of the 50s, I’m like, okay, my photo of that thing may also look plucked out of the 50s or have 50s vibe modern spin on it. I think a lot of people who shoot the kinds of subjects that I shoot often end up depicting the imagery in a way that makes me dour, because you feel the loss that has come from time. And I’m more trying to celebrate time itself and not necessarily show something in its worst state. What is it you want someone to take from a photo of one of those motels? What do you want your audience to feel? I want them to feel like they’re looking at a postcard they found in a drawer that has some handwriting on the back. I want someone to feel transported. That’s the main thing for me, whether it’s because it’s particularly alluring or because there are elements in the light and color that draw them in, I want them to feel like, “oh wow, I’m standing there.” Especially because the Polaroid format brings unreality into the mix, but have it still feel like this is an artifact of something. Like when you go into a museum and you look at an old image, it brings you there for a moment. There’s that one big Polaroid you took of, you know, the Manhattan skyline. What is it you want someone to take from that? Because that’s slightly different than trying to preserve a feeling. It is, it is different. That image in particular was interesting…I grew up in Manhattan. And my memory of going to the top of buildings and overlooking things is colored with a bit of the stuff that your memory sprinkles onto images. And getting the opportunity to even be in the position to take that photo was very fortunate. And I felt, because I had that opportunity, I wanted to make something that had an almost dream-like, almost gothic, heightened look to it. That’s what I was pulling from in my own memory because I could have taken that picture 10 minutes later, it would have looked completely different. 10 minutes earlier, would have looked completely different. I took the photo in that moment because that was the feeling I got in that moment of the light and the way the buildings looked. One thing I don’t know if I’ve heard before is how you got into Polaroid specifically? Well, Polaroid has been around me so much and I’ve used it so much over my lifetime, through elementary school, into high school. It being a thing that I would bring to the last day of school or, you know, it was an accessory that my mom basically would put in my hands and say, “now go to school” and/or “now go see a friend.” “I want lunch.” “No son, no lunch, but I did buy you this 10-pack of film.” Growing up around it, and having handled it so much growing up, I grew to associate it with a lot of things and a lot of key moments in my life. As I grew as a photographer and entered the professional field, I entered a malaise that a lot of people are familiar with, where you’re using digital tools so much in your professional life, and you use those same tools in your personal work, you start to lose some sort of connection. You think, “what am I actually doing? Is this enjoyable? What am I missing here?” Then my mom reintroduced me to it, she got me an Instax Mini right in the early Impossible era, and I fell in love with it again. I was using it solely as a party thing, it took me a few years to realize it might be the missing piece. There is something that I was looking for that I wasn’t getting out of pointing a sensor at a person or an object ,that I began getting from the magic of a Polaroid, and that switch flipped immediately. It was not a gradual thing, it was like, “okay, this is related to my past, this is related to my future, this is something I’m connecting with on a tactile level,” and I think it just clicked. From then on, pretty much, it’s been a daily driver. Do you remember when that was? I think that was probably 2016. That was when I started. And the photos from that time are still not particularly artistic, or don’t necessarily match up to what I’m doing now, but they were the early stages of starting to understand this feeling. And it took years for it to grow. Probably seven years ago is when I really snapped into it and started seeking things that I thought would be perfect for Polaroid. Why do you think that change happened? I mean, this is such a bad answer, but this is the honest truth. I had been shooting Canon digital cameras forever. And I got a Panasonic GH4 for video production. And as a result of that, switching over systems, I started using it as a photo camera. That basically deleted my interest in photography. I literally stopped taking photos and I didn’t even consciously realize why it had happened. In picking up the Polaroid again, and starting to apply it, that’s when the switch flipped. I had totally lost this thing, and it came surging back. From then on I was completely Polaroid-pilled. When you look at kind of those early Polaroids, do you understand what that evolution was for yourself? It was so abrupt in some ways that I feel like I immediately was seeking what I’m still seeking today. So the evolution has been more in methodology than what I actually was seeking through Polaroid. I’m getting the same thing that I got from it, you know, in 2018 or whatever that was. How I’m going about it has changed, my techniques have changed. But the actual core driver is basically the same. I’m 33 years old, turning 34 shortly, and I’ve gone through many periods of my life with obsessive interest in certain things. I really am obsessive about the things that I love. Cocaine/photographs/traveling. Exactly. But this started as something where I was wondering, “is this a phase? Is this something that is scratching an itch right now that is eventually going to sort of fade a little bit?” But it didn’t. It only grew. It grew even more when I started meeting people that were associated with the product’s creation, other people who use it, finding that community element, and finding an audience as well, people who want to even look at my images, and that are interested in techniques and how I did certain things. It all fed in together.   How has your work changed since becoming popular in the Polaroid community? It’s encouraged me to push myself. I think I’m very self-competitive, very self versus self. I’m constantly trying to improve and seek the next great thing that I can do. Having community, having people that react to things that I’m doing live, it helps keep me honest about all those things and keeps me more focused, because it’s arbitrary. It’s not commercial mainstream popularity. It’s all something on an app or someone in a comment section or friends, but it’s still a motivator and still a guide for me to think, “okay, I can’t not post for the next two months. I’ve got to make something today.” Even being part of the 1212 project, it’s once a month, you’ve got to do something. And having that little kick is important. It’s important for freelancers. I’m a professional freelancer. You constantly need a kick in the butt. Do you find that it pushes you artistically? During your trip to China, of course, there’s, “I want to go to these places. I want to talk to these people.” Is it also in your head, “I want to take these kinds of photos.” Yes, to a degree. China was an interesting one because I was limited in what I actually chose to do. I was essentially guided through the experience. How did the China trip come about? In June 2025, I received an email shortly after a photo convention, from a man in China who had commissioned a brand new 20×24 Polaroid camera. That’s an astronomical endeavor to me, because the film has been discontinued for 17 years. But this man sent me an email, told me he was a big fan of my YouTube channel, felt like we were kindred spirits, that we needed to immediately start talking about Polaroid, we need to start chatting. And if the mood strikes, I’m invited to Shanghai whenever I want, he can show me the city, we can make it an In An Instant episode. He basically just threw it all out there, wrote the email, and I just couldn’t let it go. The thought of doing that was so interesting to me. As someone who’s always seeking, I was like, “well, this is an interesting thing to go out and do and an adventure that could change my life.” A few months pass, I get my visa, and I go out there. I met probably a hundred different people, I was constantly being introduced to artists, to people in the government, constantly going to interesting places and completely foreign places.. I had never been in Asia, so it was a true culture shock. And I find that culture shock is difficult to experience these days because of our exposure to literally everything that’s ever happened. It was an actual genuine experience that was surprising in every corner. And to your earlier question, on day two, we got back to our hoteland we’re like, “what are we doing here? What exactly are we trying to show here? Did we, in those first two days, actually do anything that would provide value to people, or did we just nod our heads and go along with the next thing that was happening?” And from that point on, we started pushing more against something we were being presented or, for example, we were introduced to a bunch of cosplayers and someone was taking their photos and the guy I was with was like, “here, you can take the photos of the cosplayers as well. You definitely should jump in there and do that.” And I was thinking about it, that’s not really my thing, I stepped away. A few minutes later we circled back to it and I was like, “I gotta be honest. I’m more interested in the human beings that I can more easily relate to and potentially are more interesting because they are authentically themselves in this moment, versus someone who is portraying a character or essentially modeling.” I was much more interested in photographing the photographer, this crazy guy who brought five boxes of Polaroid 8×10 film on a Wednesday to this shoot. Once I peeled that layer back, I got to have this unbelievable relationship with this guy, Leo, who was the one shooting the cosplayers in the first place. I kept pushing us to fight against shooting pure artifice and try to get something a little bit more humanistic. Ultimately that was the most important thing to me, both in the images and the video. And I think it’s something we actually accomplished, which under that level of stress and moving as quickly as we were, I think that’s an interesting accomplishment. I’m pretty proud of that. When you guys are were the Great Wall of China, you definitely seemed to have a strong idea of what you wanted to capture. What did you want from those pictures? That’s a good example…as we were all on the train going to the Great Wall, we were discussing it. What do we want to do there? We’re going to be under pressure. Security is going to be coming after us. This is unsanctioned, to a degree, and we just need to go out there and do it. And under that strain, it’s difficult to think, “how do I want to organize a frame? What am I exactly trying to show here?” But I was interested in taking the Polaroid frame and creating a standalone object that is aesthetically interesting and well-organized. Something that you could put on a wall as a memento of the Great Wall of China. Whether or not we captured it on that day is in question, because it was very difficult and we lost several frames because we were trying to process the film at the Great Wall. But in a lot of these instances where you’re in this completely foreign place that has been photographed a bajillion times, one of the most critical elements to me is, maybe it’s been done a billion times, but they’re not me standing here with film that’s been expired for 20 years, where no one knows exactly what it’s going to look like. No one is going to be able to create this image other than me right now. And that’s part of the magic to me of Polaroid, you’ve got this alchemy of a person taking the photo plus this image that is also a living, breathing one-of-a-kind object. That’s what gets me excited about shooting even the most generic thing. And I think I brought home stuff that’s…at least it’s my stuff, even if it’s been done, you know, by tourists over generations. So for you, the tools that you use provide a lot of your voice. I would say so. I am easily overwhelmed by the notion of that idea, of every subject being shot before and that everyone’s seen everything before. But creating something that has a unique imprint is doable in a billion ways. As photographers, we know this, you can manipulate light, you can manipulate your subject. But for me, when you’re shooting something that’s kind of an objective scene, such as the Great Wall of China, it’s not going to pose for you. You have to take your tools and make something that is at least somewhat unique to you that, in many ways, is tied to the format itself. When there’s human beings involved, you’ve got a little bit of a different equation. And we did a lot of portraiture out there. But again, they were under these interesting conditions where you can’t really communicate well with the person you’re shooting. You can only move them so much. In some cases, we were shooting people that were nearing 100 years-old. They are fragile! They might break! Yeah, they might break. Just as delicate as the camera. In those cases, I’m leaning into the format itself as my mode of expression, because I feel that it lends a uniqueness to whatever you’re doing. If you’re taking a photo of this 95 year-old cherished artist, he’s never been shot like this before, you know, even if it’s even if it’s a resting expression portrait, it still has captured his soul in a way that’s unique in the modern day. The tools and myself go very hand in hand. We hold hands skipping down the beach. When you were studying film and photography in school, are there photographers who are touchstones in your mind when you’re making art? I don’t use photographers as a guide. Because my origins were more filmmaking-based, you know, I learned on Tarantino and Christopher Nolan and Stanley Kubrick and a lot of David Lynch, a lot of core filmmakers drove my early interest in making visual art. So when my photography branched from video, I didn’t necessarily gain new inspiration. A lot of what drove me originally and what I thought would become my main canvas was depicting cinematic scenes with photography. That was what I was originally interested in doing. And to a degree, I do find Route 66, mid-century America, very cinematic. When you just look at the film Paris, Texas, you can map some of my photos onto that film. You know, I love Stephen Shore as much as the next guy, but I don’t necessarily look at his images and think I gotta go get out there right now. I more look at my own images and think, oh, I gotta get out there right now and make something that is more true to me or is better than the last thing. Do you have people that inspire you, now? I would say, someone like Fred Johnson, who is a Polaroid guy, he makes these miniatures of himself and puts them into miniature scenes. And while that is completely different than the type of thing that I would do, I love the way he’s baking reality into unreality. That is something that I try at least once a month, as part of the 1212 project, because it’s an excuse to experiment. And so that, his style, the kinds of things he’s doing, it’s inspiring, especially through Polaroid, which adds this additional layer of almost confusion, when you’re looking at a scene that is real, but something is off a little bit, the chemistry is melting that all together. I’m obsessed with Jamie Swick and her work. I find myself in nature very often as a result of being in these unusual places. And her work and her ability to create emotion out of a tree, or ind the color in something that I wouldn’t normally look closely at, she encourages me to be much more observant. Honestly, and this is aspirational, but Walter Iooss. He’s one of the greatest sports photographers of all times and he’s taken some of the most unbelievable images of athletes that I’ve ever seen. He’s a constant inspiration to me. Ironically, I work with athletes almost every day, shooting video, but the photo element only comes in now and again. And so that’s sort of an aspirational one where I look at him and it pushes me to want to go out and do that. And figure out, how am I gonna do that? That’s something I want to do more of going forward, because it really is the marriage of my two biggest interests. How has your YouTube project, In An Instant , influenced your photography? I don’t think it has had a direct impact on the images that I make. More it’s given me the opportunity to explore what goes into the images with much more depth, and has given me a layer of consciousness that I didn’t have before, where every time I publish something, I’m thinking about the layers of it, how it’s perceived, how I created it, what tools were used to make it, what I meant to do when I made it. It gets me excited to make work, it’s another motivator, because it’s like, all right, we’re making a video about the SX-70 right now. I have a thousand photos I’ve taken with it in the past, but I’d rather go out right now and take a thousand more. Right now I’m testing a new SX-70 modification. I’ve used the SX-70 a thousand times, but it’s making me very stoked to go out the door and go find something. In An Instant gives me these excuses to do that with my everyday life. And as a freelancer, thankfully, I have pockets of time to explore that. What’s your favorite photo that you’ve taken? I mean, the Manhattan skyline photo is an interesting one because it does feel so fundamental to me. It feels like a bio photo or like if I died, they would show it. Alongside that, I also have a couple of 8×10 images of my grandfather that are particularly special. He was an artist, he was a hand illustrator, he was an actor, and I was following all these levels of his life when I was growing up, and then to end up…he’s 93 years old. I’m taking his 8×10 right now. That just felt like sort of this natural photo that had to be made, and so to have done that with him was really special, and so that photo is particularly core to me. There’s another recent one, which was just my wife’s house at Christmas time, doing a long exposure of the family with the tree. Again, it felt like a personal memory that I’m going to look back on in 50 years and be able to just be standing right there. The camera and that process helps me ground myself in those moments and helps me place myself in time, as well. I’m really overactive and I really do so much. Everything can start blurring together, but when I look at one of those images I’m like, okay, I remember what it smelled like, I remember what my feet felt like standing there, so those three I think immediately come to mind. They also happen to be directly in front of me. Top three photos I can see. What is it about the 8×10 versus, you know, a regular Polaroid, you know, or a 4×5? I think the 8×10 is, first of all, it’s a more unique and true replication of a person or a place because of the field of view and because of what the lensing is doing. It’s a more natural POV than light coming through a cone and then going into a very small place. It’s giving you this more natural scale replica of reality, which in the end I think is one of the core things that I’m after. And then there’s also this intimacy that happens when you’re shooting either a person or a place. The amount of time you’re standing there and considering things and making the tiniest little movements and changes of focus. Those all just make it a more interesting experience to me and I think the images are always reflective of that because you feel like you can’t blow it if you if you throw up an 8×10, like, it screws up your day and maybe even your life. So it puts this extra onus on the actual process of it that you get that feeling with a typical Polaroid picture because it is so special. But I think it’s different with 8×10 and it just hits different than when you’re holding a 4×5. It’s still this small thing. With the 8×10 the fact that you can hold it and you’re just like, bam, that is in your face. It’s such a special experience, especially when you’re doing it with someone else. You get this core moment where you’re both looking at this object and you’re just like. “wow, how is this even possible?” Those moments are so hard to come by. We’re in this ridiculous time and actually having a moment of genuine “whoa”. I’m always chasing that. When you are photographing someone, is it helpful having that laborious process? How does that affect what you’re going for with a portrait? As someone with the cinematography background, the feeling of setting up the lights carefully orchestrating the environment that you’re in, you’re not necessarily just being like, “hey, can you stand there? Boom.” You’re organizing the environment, the light, and the person. It’s more romantic for everyone involved. It helps bring whatever I’m trying to bring out of that person because they feel like they’re in a movie almost, they feel like they’re in the 1800s with this gigantic camera and they want to be involved and give you something that you haven’t gone before. It can be hard to make someone feel comfortable in that circumstance. I’ve definitely encountered people who are like, “I’m like standing still for a minute. I can’t do this.” That’s part of the challenge of it. But when it works, there just isn’t a feeling like it. I’m always trying to chase that. Do you have a sense of what it is you want from a subject when you’re trying to take a portrait? Yeah, I’m just trying to bring out the core beauty of somebody, show them in…I want to take the funeral photo. I want to take the beautiful, stately picture of somebody on this large format that represents them like no other and give them an art object of themselves. I think that’s what I’m looking for more than, “oh, she’s really happy. She should be smiling.” I am trying to bring something out of someone that might not necessarily be the most basic thing. Subtly and with light and with lens and with their eyes and all of those elements. Now, what do you have planned for the future? Well I’ve gotten into the Chinese market. “I work for the Chinese government now.” It’s becoming a bit of a thing! I’m going to be exploring China more next year. Now that I’ve built relationships that allow me access that I wouldn’t have had before. That’s exciting to me as an artist and as a modern man. Being able to turn over pages that have been stuck together for 70 years and being able to actually see something genuinely fresh and new and experience that with someone and photograph them, that’s a cocktail for me. So that is something I want to do going forward. In terms of the video/photo combined element, I think I’m transitioning into a slightly more docu-style in general, whether that’s what I’m trying to depict on my YouTube channel or the photos that I’m taking alongside that. I’m finding myself doing street photography a little more. I’m finding myself taking documents of a place that aren’t as orchestrated by myself by time of day and light and waiting for the right moment. Sometimes the moment itself is enough and that is sort of what I’m transitioning into. But yeah, going more into docu-stuff, exploring China, going to other countries and becoming more globally-minded, my last 8 years have been really America focused. Honestly, my last 15 years. Honestly, my whole life. My last 33 years. Honestly, my whole fucking life has been entrenched in the Americana aesthetic. And so expanding that and being more globally-focused in what I’m doing is really piquing my interest right now. I’m going to keep leaning into that. The China trip was really transformative for you. It really was. It really was. I mean, it’s one of those generic things to say, but it totally did change me and show me a different way. Not necessarily because they directly showed me something I should be doing, but just because I was thrown into this atmosphere that was much different than I’m used to and it forced me to adjust in ways that I ended up liking a lot. The feeling of waking up in the morning and being like, “holy shit, what are we doing today? How are we going to do this today?” This is a photo/video super-challenge. I’m now lusting for that again. I recently went to Japan, did something similar, not as tortured as having to navigate the challenges I had to navigate in China. Them all being good, of course, but I did this in Japan. I believe I’m going to the Netherlands soon, headed to Scotland in the fall and who knows what else going forward, but I’m hoping to use those opportunities to do some more exploration-documentation and meet some people and take some crazy portraits. Which do you prefer, the process or the result? The result. I find that reflecting on images I’ve taken, it makes me happy. It makes me really happy. And I’ve always thought like, when that stops happening, I need to do something else. Because when I look at my own folder of images, I almost always have a freaking smile on my face. I’m living through my own life in this oddly linear way. Just through the process of taking photos every day and trying to capture whatever the keystone moment is of this day or this trip or this time. And I think the result is, it’s going through and experiencing these personal emotions, even if they never reach outside of myself. And ultimately, like I said, I’m self-competitive. I don’t care that much what someone thinks about my work or what I’m doing. I’m mostly just chasing that feeling of reflecting and thinking, “damn, I did it the way I wanted to do it. I’m very proud of that. It’s on my wall. I’m staring at it. I’m picking my favorite three photos on the wall.” That’s what I’m after. That joie de vivre… Yes, exactly. I started experiencing…well, I noticed a lack of it in when I was growing up. I was looking at our family photos, I was looking at the pictures we were making of ourselves as a family. Several people in my family are photographers and several of them stopped shooting once the digital transition happened. I noticed this broad gap that started to grow in the family photos. I don’t have any photos of myself from age 10 to 13 or whatever. It’s just bizarre. Once I started noticing that, I was like, “I need to start filling in these gaps.” And that has never left me, that feeling of needing to create some sort of chronology of life and have some sort of record of life. And a lot of that also stems from my continuous introspection growing up about our place in the universe. It’s an interesting thought…you noticed that it wasn’t happening and that you felt that was bad. Yeah, it was kind of horrifying. And it was kind of scary. There’s no record of… What was scary about it? It was scary to not have any record of existence and not have…I am very nostalgia-obsessed, and by that I mean, I like staring at something and feeling what it felt like to be there and think of all the elements that went into the moment and not being able to have access to any of that was scary because, you know, my memory is however good it is, but it’s, it’s not as good as a picture and it’s not as good as being able to travel through a picture into your mind palace and place yourself in that moment. And I was scared by the lack of any record of any of it. What is it that draws you to that feeling of nostalgia? I think about this all the time. That phrase, “nostalgia is a drug,” I actually feel like a chemical thing when I’m going through time in my mind. And I’ve always been chasing that feeling. It’s like, I’m trying to actually put it into words. It’s hard to put into words. But I remember when my Aunt Kibbe was dying, she was like 99 years-old, and I was thinking, “this is going to be inaccessible in my mind, this space, this time, if I don’t do something about it.” Or when I was moving out of college and I was thinking, “this apartment is insane, it’s a piece of shit. But if I don’t do something about that and start filming it or take photos of it, then I’ll have no way to reflect back on this.” And I do honestly think it has to do with this thought I had growing up of, “what is our place in the world? What is the impermanence of humanity? We are so irrelevant in the grand scheme of things, so we have to create some sort of trail for ourselves. Otherwise, none of this matters.” And I do think that that has very much..that’s just in my blood. Nostalgia is connected to that. Being able to access the past, knowing that it’s gone, is a superpower. I mean, to you, it feels like if you don’t record it, you’ll lose it. Yeah, 100%. 100%, I do feel like it’s lost. And I don’t trust my own memory to have the detailed… I don’t trust my own memory and I don’t trust my own process of being alive to be able to encase life itself without that. And now I don’t fear it anymore because I obsessively do it. But I think when you see people shooting endlessly on iPhones or photos going to cloud storage, I think almost the same thing is happening. Yes, you can sit there and scroll through your phone, but you will lose that. That will go away. Whether or not that’s now or in 200 years, no one’s going to open up a cardboard box and find your old clothes and your phone in there and wake up your cloud library. It’s just not going to happen. And so making these physical objects, especially through Polaroid, is that immediate moment of creation and installation and piece of nostalgia you can hold forever until it fades away. But, you know, everything will fade away eventually. I mean…you just fear death. Let’s just get it out there! Well yeah! What’s funny is, I didn’t fear death growing up. I was very emboldened for some reason. I was very aware of death and that it was going to come and I think it’s not necessarily fear of dying, it’s a fear of dying and nothing’s there when you’re dead, oblivion, there’s no Ben anymore after he dies, but there may be this register of his life that, if someone bothers to, they can go through and access it. And I think that is weirdly intangible for many people, and I am creating something tangible so that it doesn’t happen to me. It’s not death, it’s being forgotten. It’s that if you’re not remembered, it doesn’t matter. Yeah, if you’re not remembered and if there’s no trail, if there’s no trace, that is scary to me. I think that this all ties into the stuff that I like shooting, because when I’m out on Route 66 or I’m out in the middle of America and I’m out in these random places that even the most well-drawn collector of old sites has seen, I do feel like the Polaroid and this process is doing that thing. It’s taking the world that is disappearing and is constantly changing and that we’ll have no trace of and it’s making a physical thing of it. And same with a portrait of a person. When I say I want to take the funeral photo, that’s what I’m talking about. Taking this image that is emblematic and can be looked back on and it leaves a trace and it leaves a record. And it’s a classical concept. It’s something that was basically started with the very first realistic paintings, but that is the kind of thing I’m after. It’s the encapsulation. Related

Entrevista 098 • 25 de mayo 2026

  • Entrevista y Retrato de Ben Fraternale por Lou Noble

Acerca de Ben Fraternale

Ben Fraternale es un artista multidisciplinar de Nueva York impulsado por un entusiasmo infinito por la creatividad y las imágenes móviles. Ha trabajado con Delta, la NBA, Nespresso, Polaroid, Brooklyn Film Camera, IBM, Bed Bath & Beyond, GM, Verizon, Comprar Bebé, Mars-Wrigley y muchos otros.

  • Sitio web »
  • Blog personal »
  • Flickr »
  • Instagram »

Prefacio

La fotografía, la fotografía real, es sobre la pérdida. La cara a lo largo de una década. El cartel del motel en una carretera del condado en Nuevo México que será una losa de fundación y algunas malas hierbas en cinco años. Todo lo que amas, olvidado. La mayoría de los fotógrafos lo fotografian y lo llaman nostalgia. Ben Fraternale lo fotografia como un hombre tratando de superar su propio fallecimiento.

Tiene treinta y tres años, vive en Nueva York, ha construido una carrera en una obra de cine que ha estado a punto desde que estaba en el instituto, y quiere, en sus propias palabras, tomar tu foto funeraria.
-Agustin Sánchez
-...
Esta entrevista ha sido editada para claridad y contenido.

Entrevista

Cuando estás tomando fotos ahora mismo, ¿qué es lo que estás tratando de hacer?

Es una cosa en constante evolución. Un día soy un conservacionista, otro día estoy tomando fotos de personas y conduciendo alegría de eso, pero creo, en última instancia, que estoy impulsado por la necesidad de inculcar momentos e imágenes en el tiempo, y algo sobre eso es núcleo para mi persona. Cómo eso se manifiesta en las imágenes mismas no es necesariamente tan vívidamente claro para mí, pero siempre estoy tratando de robar un momento, en particular camino

Me encanta constantemente buscar y aventurar y conducir durante horas, buscando cosas que a veces nunca encuentro, pero cuando encuentro esa cosa, si puedo capturar ese momento en el tiempo y hacer algo atemporal, creo que eso es lo que estoy buscando.

Y se manifiesta en una variedad de maneras. Creo que con Polaroid, es el formato perfecto para hacerlo porque creas algo físico fuera de la realidad en un instante. Terminas con este objeto físico de un lugar, especialmente con el formato Polaroid 8×10. Eso es parte de por qué me encanta ese formato tal vez el más, porque es el ejemplo final de esto. Es el más cercano “ahorro” de un momento que siempre puedes cambiar.

Cuando estás haciendo la Ruta 66 imágenes y mirando viejos moteles, ¿sabes qué es lo que estás buscando cuando lo ves?

Sí, realmente lo hago. Hay una línea fina en mis viajes, entre algo que es decrépito y me hace sentir triste, y algo que parece que alguien ha puesto cuidado en mantener algún tipo de presencia visual, una estética que en realidad está preservando ese lugar.

A veces me atrae algo que está en ruinas o tiene una condición particularmente interesante. Pero creo que, en su mayoría, cuando veo un motel que parece arrancado de los años 50, soy como, vale, mi foto de esa cosa también puede parecer arrancada de los años 50 o tener 50 vibración moderna en ella.

Creo que mucha gente que dispara los tipos de temas que dispare a menudo termina representando la imagen de una manera que me hace dour, porque sientes la pérdida que ha venido de vez en cuando. Y estoy más tratando de celebrar el tiempo en sí mismo y no necesariamente mostrar algo en su peor estado.

¿Qué es lo que quieres que alguien tome de una foto de uno de esos moteles? ¿Qué quieres que sienta tu audiencia?

Quiero que se sientan como si estuvieran viendo una postal que encontraron en un cajón que tiene alguna escritura en la espalda. Quiero que alguien se sienta transportado. Esa es la cosa principal para mí, ya sea porque es particularmente atractivo o porque hay elementos en la luz y el color que los dibujan, quiero que se sientan como, "oh wow, estoy parado allí mezclar." Especialmente porque el museo Polaroid viejo se ve un artefacto

Hay una gran Polaroid de la que tomaste, ya sabes, el horizonte de Manhattan. ¿Qué es lo que quieres que alguien tome de eso? Porque eso es un poco diferente que tratar de preservar un sentimiento.

Es, es diferente. Esa imagen en particular era interesante... Crecí en Manhattan. Y mi memoria de ir a la cima de los edificios y de las cosas que miran se coloreó con un poco de las cosas que su memoria rocia sobre las imágenes. Y conseguir la oportunidad de estar incluso en la posición de tomar esa foto era muy afortunado. Y sentí, porque tenía esa oportunidad, quería hacer algo que tenía un momento casi de sueño, casi gótico, alto

Una cosa que no sé si he oído antes es cómo te metiste en Polaroid específicamente?

Bueno, Polaroid ha estado a mi alrededor tanto y lo he utilizado tanto durante mi vida, a través de la escuela primaria, en la secundaria. Es una cosa que yo traería al último día de la escuela o, ya sabes, era un accesorio que mi madre básicamente me pusiera en las manos y decir, "ahora ir a la escuela" y/o "ahora ir a ver a un amigo."

“Quiero comer”.

"Ningún hijo, ningún almuerzo, pero te compré esta 10-palabra de película." Creciendo alrededor de ella, y habiendo manejado tanto crecer, crecí para asociarlo con muchas cosas y muchos momentos clave en mi vida. Mientras crecí como fotógrafo y entraba en el campo profesional, entré en un malestar con el que mucha gente está familiarizada, donde estás usando herramientas digitales tanto en tu vida profesional, y que usas esas herramientas tempranamente

Lo estaba usando sólo como una cosa de fiesta, me tomó unos años darme cuenta de que podría ser la pieza perdida. Hay algo que estaba buscando que no estaba saliendo de apuntar un sensor a una persona o un objeto, que empecé a conseguir de la magia de un Polaroid, y que el interruptor se volteó inmediatamente. No era una cosa gradual, era como, “okay, esto está relacionado con mi pasado, este nivel está relacionado con el futuro

¿Recuerdas cuando fue eso?

Creo que fue probablemente 2016. Eso fue cuando empecé. Y las fotos de ese tiempo todavía no son particularmente artísticas, o no necesariamente coinciden con lo que estoy haciendo ahora, pero eran las primeras etapas de empezar a entender este sentimiento. Y tomó años para que crezca. Probablemente hace siete años es cuando realmente me atrapé en ella y empecé a buscar cosas que pensé que serían perfectas para Polaroid.

¿Por qué crees que pasó ese cambio?

Quiero decir, esta es una mala respuesta, pero esta es la verdad honesta. Había estado filmando cámaras digitales Canon para siempre. Y conseguí un GH4 Panasonic para la producción de video. Y como resultado de eso, cambiando sistemas, empecé a usarlo como una cámara fotográfica. Eso básicamente borró mi interés en la fotografía. Literalmente dejé de tomar fotos y ni siquiera me di cuenta conscientemente por qué había sucedido.

Cuando miras como esos primeros Polaroids, ¿entiendes qué es eso?
¿La evolución era para ti?

Fue tan abrupto de alguna manera que siento que inmediatamente estaba buscando lo que todavía estoy buscando hoy. Así que la evolución ha sido más en la metodología que lo que realmente estaba buscando a través de Polaroid. Estoy recibiendo la misma cosa que he conseguido de ella, ya sabes, en 2018 o lo que fuera. Cómo voy a hacerlo ha cambiado, mis técnicas han cambiado. Pero el conductor verdadero es básicamente el mismo. Tengo 33 años de interés poco tiempo que girar la vida

Cocaína/fotografías/traveling.

Exactamente. Pero esto comenzó como algo en lo que me preguntaba, ¿es una fase? ¿Es esto algo que está rascando una picazón ahora mismo que finalmente va a hacer un poco de moda? Pero no lo hizo. Creció aún más cuando empecé a conocer gente que estaba asociada con la creación del producto, otras personas que lo utilizan, encontrando ese elemento comunitario, y encontrando un público también, personas que quieren y hasta miran mis imágenes.

 

¿Cómo ha cambiado su trabajo desde que se populariza en la comunidad Polaroid?

Me anima a empujar a mí mismo. Creo que soy muy auto-competitivo, muy auto versus uno mismo. Estoy constantemente tratando de mejorar y buscar la próxima gran cosa que puedo hacer. Tener comunidad, tener gente que reacciona a las cosas que estoy haciendo en vivo, ayuda a mantenerme honesto sobre todas esas cosas y me mantiene más enfocado, porque es arbitrario. No es popularidad comercial principal.

¿Te parece que te empuja artísticamente? Durante tu viaje a China, por supuesto, hay, “Quiero ir a estos lugares. Quiero hablar con esta gente.” Es también en tu cabeza, “Quiero tomar este tipo de fotos”.

Sí, hasta cierto punto. China era una interesante porque estaba limitada en lo que realmente elegí hacer. Fui guiado esencialmente a través de la experiencia.

¿Cómo ocurrió el viaje a China?

En junio de 2025, recibí un correo electrónico poco después de una convención fotográfica, de un hombre en China que había encargado una nueva cámara Polaroid de 20×24. Eso es un esfuerzo astronómico para mí, porque la película ha sido suspendida durante 17 años.

Pero este hombre me envió un correo electrónico, me dijo que era un gran fan de mi canal de YouTube, se sentía como si fuéramos espíritus amistosos, que necesitábamos empezar a hablar inmediatamente de Polaroid, necesitamos empezar a charlar. Y si el estado de ánimo golpea, estoy invitado a Shanghai cuando quiera, él puede mostrarme la ciudad, podemos hacer un episodio de In An Instant. Él básicamente lo dejó todo allí, escribió el correo electrónico, y yo simplemente fuera

Pasan unos meses, recibo mi visa, y salgo allí. Conocí probablemente a cien personas diferentes, estaba constantemente siendo presentado a artistas, a personas en el gobierno, constantemente yendo a lugares interesantes y lugares completamente extranjeros.. Nunca había estado en Asia, por lo que fue un verdadero choque cultural. Y encuentro que el choque cultural es difícil de experimentar estos días debido a nuestra exposición a literalmente todo lo que ha sucedido. Fue una verdadera experiencia que fue sorprendente en cada esquina.

Y a su pregunta anterior, el día dos, regresamos a nuestro hotel y somos como, “¿qué estamos haciendo aquí? ¿Qué es exactamente lo que intentamos mostrar aquí? ¿Hemos hecho, en esos dos primeros días, algo que proporcionaría valor a la gente, o simplemente hemos dado cuenta de nuestras cabezas y nos hemos unido a lo siguiente que estaba sucediendo?” Y desde ese punto en adelante, empezamos a empujar más fácilmente contra algo que nos estaban presentando o, por ejemplo

Estaba mucho más interesado en fotografiar al fotógrafo, este loco que trajo cinco cajas de la película Polaroid 8×10 en un miércoles a esta sesión. Una vez que pelé esa capa atrás, tengo que tener esta increíble relación con este tipo, Leo, que fue el que disparó a los cosplayers en primer lugar. Yo seguía empujando a luchar contra el tiro de arte puro y tratar de conseguir algo un poco más humanista.

Cuando ustedes eran la Gran Muralla de China, definitivamente parecían tener una idea fuerte de lo que querían capturar. ¿Qué querían de esas fotos?

Es un buen ejemplo... ya que todos estábamos en el tren yendo a la Gran Muralla, lo estábamos discutiendo. ¿Qué queremos hacer allí? Vamos a estar bajo presión. La seguridad va a venir después de nosotros. Esto es sin sanción, hasta cierto grado, y sólo tenemos que salir allí y hacerlo. Y bajo esa tensión, es difícil pensar, “¿cómo quiero organizar un marco estético?

Si lo capturamos o no en ese día está en cuestión, porque fue muy difícil y perdimos varios marcos porque estábamos tratando de procesar la película en la Gran Muralla. Pero en muchas de estas instancias donde estás en este lugar completamente extranjero que ha sido fotografiado un millón de veces, uno de los elementos más críticos para mí es, tal vez se ha hecho mil millones de veces, pero no soy yo parado aquí con película que ha sido vencida durante 20 años, donde nadie sabe exactamente cómo va a parecer.

Nadie va a ser capaz de crear esta imagen aparte de mí en este momento. Y eso es parte de la magia para mí de Polaroid, tienes esta alquimia de una persona tomando la foto más esta imagen que también es un objeto vivo, respirando uno de la especie. Eso es lo que me excita disparar incluso la cosa más genérica. Y creo que traje cosas de casa que es ... al menos es mi cosa turistas, incluso se hace

Así que para ti, las herramientas que utilizas proporcionan mucha voz.

Yo diría que sí. Estoy fácilmente abrumado por la noción de esa idea, de cada tema que se le disparó antes y que todo el mundo lo ha visto todo antes. Pero crear algo que tiene una impresión única es factible de mil millones de maneras. Como fotógrafos, sabemos esto, usted puede manipular la luz, usted puede manipular su tema. Pero para mí, cuando usted está filmando algo que es una especie de escena objetiva, como la Gran Muralla de China que no va

Usted tiene que tomar sus herramientas y hacer algo que es por lo menos un poco único para usted que, de muchas maneras, está ligado al formato mismo. Cuando hay seres humanos involucrados, usted tiene un poco de una ecuación diferente. Y hicimos un montón de retratos allí fuera. Pero de nuevo, ellos estaban bajo estas condiciones interesantes donde realmente no se puede comunicar bien con la persona que está filmando. Sólo se puede mover cerca de ellos tanto.

¡Son frágiles!

Sí, pueden romperse. Tan delicado como la cámara. En esos casos, me estoy inclinando en el formato mismo como mi modo de expresión, porque siento que presta una singularidad a lo que estás haciendo. Si estás tomando una foto de este artista de 95 años, nunca ha sido disparado como este antes, ya sabes, incluso si es un día de reposo de expresión de alma capturada, todavía tiene una mano de esquiar

Cuando estabas estudiando cine y fotografía en la escuela, ¿hay fotógrafos que son piedras táctiles en tu mente cuando estás haciendo arte?

No uso los fotógrafos como guía. Debido a que mis orígenes eran más basados en el cine, ya sabes, aprendí en Tarantino y Christopher Nolan y Stanley Kubrick y muchos de David Lynch, muchos de los cineastas principales condujeron mi primer interés en hacer arte visual. Así que cuando mi fotografía ramificó de vídeo, no necesariamente conseguía inspiración.

¿Tienes gente que te inspire?

Yo diría, alguien como Fred Johnson, que es un tipo Polaroid, él hace estas miniaturas de sí mismo y las pone en escenas de miniatura. Y mientras que eso es completamente diferente al tipo de cosa que haría, me encanta la forma en que está horneando la realidad en la irrealidad. Eso es algo que intento al menos una vez al mes, como parte del proyecto 1212, porque es una excusa para experimentar su estilo.

Estoy obsesionado con Jamie Swick y su trabajo. Me encuentro en la naturaleza muy a menudo como resultado de estar en estos lugares inusuales. Y su trabajo y su habilidad para crear emoción fuera de un árbol, o ind el color en algo que normalmente no miraría de cerca, ella me anima a ser mucho más observante.

Honestamente, y esto es aspiracional, pero Walter Iooss. Él es uno de los mayores fotógrafos deportivos de todos los tiempos y él ha tomado algunas de las imágenes más increíbles de los atletas que he visto. Él es una inspiración constante para mí. Irónicamente, trabajo con atletas casi todos los días, video de disparo, pero el elemento de la foto sólo viene de vez en cuando. Y así que es una especie de interés

¿Cómo tiene su proyecto de YouTube, In An Instant¿Influyó en su fotografía?

No creo que haya tenido un impacto directo en las imágenes que hago. Más me ha dado la oportunidad de explorar lo que pasa en las imágenes con mucha más profundidad, y me ha dado una capa de conciencia que no tenía antes, donde cada vez que publico algo, estoy pensando en las capas de ella, cómo se percibe, cómo lo creé, qué herramientas se utilizaban para hacer, lo que quería hacer cuando se hace miles

¿Cuál es tu foto favorita que has tomado?

Quiero decir, la foto de Manhattan es interesante porque me hace sentir tan fundamental. Se siente como una foto bio o como si muriera, lo demostrarían. Además, también tengo un par de imágenes de 8×10 de mi abuelo que son particularmente especiales. Era un artista, era un ilustrador de manos, era un actor, y yo estaba siguiendo todos estos niveles de su vida cuando estaba creciendo, y entonces se hizo como 93 años

Hay otro reciente, que era sólo la casa de mi esposa en Navidad, haciendo una larga exposición de la familia con el árbol. Otra vez, se sintió como un recuerdo personal que voy a mirar hacia atrás en 50 años y ser capaz de estar justo ahí. La cámara y ese proceso me ayuda a aterrizar en esos momentos y me ayuda a colocarme a mí mismo en el tiempo, también. Estoy realmente sobreactivo y realmente lo hago muy borroso.

Las tres mejores fotos que puedo ver. ¿Qué pasa con el 8×10 contra, ya sabes, un Polaroid regular, ya sabes, o un 4×5?

Creo que el 8×10 es, en primer lugar, es una réplica más única y verdadera de una persona o un lugar debido al campo de visión y debido a lo que está haciendo la lente. Es un POV más natural que la luz que viene a través de un cono y luego entra en un lugar muy pequeño. Te está dando esta réplica de la realidad más natural, que al final creo que es una de las cosas básicas que estoy después de la cantidad.

Todos ellos simplemente hacen que sea una experiencia más interesante para mí y creo que las imágenes siempre son reflexivas de eso porque sientes que no puedes soplar si vomitas un 8×10, como, te arruina el día y tal vez incluso tu vida. Así que pone este extra en el proceso real de que tienes ese sentimiento con una imagen Polaroid típica porque es tan especial. Pero creo que es diferente con 8×10

Es una experiencia tan especial, especialmente cuando lo estás haciendo con alguien más. Consigues este momento central en el que ambos estás mirando este objeto y eres igual. “¿Cómo es posible esto?” Esos momentos son tan difíciles de pasar. Estamos en este momento ridículo y en realidad tener un momento de auténtica “whoa”. Siempre estoy persiguiendo eso.

Cuando estás fotografiando a alguien, ¿es útil tener ese proceso laborioso? ¿Cómo afecta eso a lo que vas a buscar con un retrato?

Como alguien con el fondo cinematográfico, la sensación de configurar las luces cuidadosamente orquestando el ambiente en el que estás, no eres necesariamente simplemente ser como, “¿puedes estar ahí? Boom.” Estás organizando el medio ambiente, la luz y la persona. Es más romántico para todos los involucrados.

Esto ayuda a traer lo que estoy tratando de sacar de esa persona porque sienten que están en una película casi, sienten que están en la década de 1800 con esta gigantesca cámara y quieren estar involucrados y darle algo que no han ido antes. Puede ser difícil hacer que alguien se sienta cómodo en esa circunstancia. Definitivamente he encontrado a personas que son como, “Soy como estar quieto por un minuto. No puedo hacer nada.

¿Tiene sentido de lo que es lo que quiere de un sujeto cuando está tratando de tomar un retrato?

Sí, solo estoy tratando de sacar la belleza central de alguien, mostrarles en... Quiero tomar la foto funeraria. Quiero tomar la imagen hermosa y estacional de alguien en este gran formato que los representa como ningún otro y darles un objeto de arte de sí mismos. Creo que eso es lo que estoy buscando más que, “oh, ella es realmente feliz. Ella debe estar sonriendo.” Estoy tratando de traer algo de alguien que no sea de la lente básica

Ahora, ¿qué has planeado para el futuro?

Bueno, he entrado en el mercado chino.

“Ahora trabajo para el gobierno chino”.

Se está convirtiendo en un poco de una cosa! Voy a estar explorando China más el próximo año. Ahora que he construido relaciones que me permiten el acceso que no habría tenido antes. Eso es excitante para mí como artista y como hombre moderno. Ser capaz de dar vuelta a páginas que han sido pegadas juntos durante 70 años y ser capaz de ver realmente algo realmente fresco y nuevo y experiencia que con alguien y fotografiarlos, que es un cóctel para mí.

En cuanto al elemento combinado video/foto, creo que estoy pasando a un estilo de docu un poco más en general, ya sea eso es lo que estoy tratando de representar en mi canal de YouTube o las fotos que estoy tomando junto a eso. Me encuentro haciendo la fotografía callejera un poco más. Me estoy encontrando tomando documentos de un lugar que no son tan orquestado por mí mismo en tiempo de día y luz y esperando el momento adecuado.

Pero sí, yendo más hacia el docu-stuff, explorando China, yendo a otros países y convirtiéndose en más globalmente, mis últimos 8 años han sido realmente América enfocada. About David LaChapelle

David LaChapelle is an American photographer and director whose work has played a defining role in shaping contemporary visual culture since the late 1980s. After being discovered by Andy Warhol and hired to work at Interview magazine, LaChapelle quickly became known for his hyper-saturated, theatrically staged photographs that bridged fashion, celebrity portraiture, and fine art.

Over the course of his career, his work has appeared in major international publications and been exhibited in museums and galleries worldwide. While his early images were often associated with pop excess and celebrity culture, LaChapelle’s practice has increasingly turned toward themes of faith, environmental anxiety, consumerism, and spiritual reckoning. His later works reflect a sustained interest in mythology, religious iconography, and the tension between spectacle and belief.

Across four decades, LaChapelle has remained committed to collaborative, labor-intensive image-making—building physical sets, painting negatives, and working with artisans whose crafts are increasingly rare. His work continues to challenge distinctions between commercial and fine art photography, insisting on the photograph as both a constructed object and a cultural mirror.

Foreword

David LaChapelle’s images are immediately recognizable: saturated, theatrical, meticulously staged, and unapologetically maximal. Emerging from the worlds of fashion magazines, pop culture, and Interview magazine under the mentorship of Andy Warhol, he has spent decades collapsing the boundaries between commercial photography, fine art, and spectacle. Beneath the surface excess lies a sustained engagement with belief systems—faith, capitalism, celebrity, environmental collapse, and the human appetite for meaning.

In recent years, those concerns have come into sharper focus. Environmental works sit alongside spiritual allegories, hand-painted negatives converse with large-scale constructed tableaus, and humor gives way to grief, anxiety, and uneasy reflection. At a moment when photography is increasingly flattened into screens, prompts, and simulations, LaChapelle continues to insist on the physical act of making images—building sets by hand, painting skies, lighting performers, and photographing scenes that exist in space and time.

I met LaChapelle surrounded by this body of work, and our conversation unfolded less like a formal interview than a sustained meditation on craft, collaboration, authorship, and survival. We spoke about analog processes in a digital age, the labor behind his most ambitious images, the role of collaboration in his studio, and how his relationship to work, faith, and balance has shifted over time.

Interview

I want to start broadly. You’ve lived through several major shifts in photography — cultural, technological, economic. When you look back at when you first started, what feels most different to you about the world when you entered versus the one you’re working in now?

Yeah. My heroes. Avedon started young, like me, working within magazines — Hearst, Condé Nast, advertising — and he died under that same system. That mattered to me when I was young, seeing that path, seeing that you could live your whole life inside photography.

Photography has changed so dramatically since I started taking pictures. First it was analog. Then Photoshop arrived. And then the internet really, really took over. I remember when people talked about what was in Vanity Fair. People actually talked about it. There were contracts — real contracts. Rolling Stone, Condé Nast Traveler — there were budgets, there was time, there was space to make things.

That entire ecosystem doesn’t really exist anymore. So I’m just grateful to still be working, honestly. And with all that change, the most important thing for me was learning how to evolve instead of fighting it. But at the same time, I’ve tried very hard to hold on to my belief in an analog vision.

People look at the work now and assume it’s AI or digitally assembled, but it isn’t. I used to hate behind-the-scenes images. I really hated them. I felt like they gave away the magic. But now I shoot behind the scenes for everything, because I want there to be proof. Proof that these images were built, not put together later on a computer.

When you say “built,” what does that actually look like for you? Why does it matter that people understand that process?

Because I believe in what I do. I really do. And the work is theatrical — it takes a lot of skill from a lot of people. Builders. Painters. Projectionists. Set designers. Lighting people. All of it.

To take all of that labor and collapse it into one digital author just isn’t fair. The credit belongs to the people who actually built these things. The Tower of Babel still sits in my studio. It’s physically there. The sky is airbrushed — that’s a dying art. I’ve worked with maybe three airbrush artists in my entire career. You just don’t find that anymore.

Those backgrounds — the airbrush painting, the lighting — those are real crafts. In the seventies there were lots of airbrush artists. Now it’s almost gone. So when someone says, “Oh, that’s just digital,” it erases the people who made it.

Those backgrounds — the airbrush painting, the lighting — those are crafts that are disappearing.  To call that a digital composite erases the labor of the people who made it.

Collaboration feels inseparable from how you work.

Completely. I want to see the tableaus exist in front of me. I’m not a computer guy. I want to see the sets, the costumes, the lighting, the casting — all of it.

There’s an adrenaline rush to that. It’s theatrical. Opening night is the shoot. The flashes go off. I cast a lot of dancers because they’re very free with their bodies. When we’re done, people cheer. It really feels like a performance.

I dream about being on sets all the time. Either I’m on a photo shoot, or I’m apartment hunting in New York. Those are my two recurring dreams.

Apartments in New York were ecstatic and traumatic at the same time. I got my first squat when I was sixteen, on Third Street between Avenue A and B in 1979. Later, I subleased it to a friend who kept it from me. People were ruthless about apartments.

I still have dreams about that — and about being on set.

Do you still carry that energy once the image is finished?

I’m addicted to that feeling during the shoot. Completely addicted. But once it’s done, I don’t really think about the process anymore unless I’m explaining it. Then it becomes about the composition. About printing.

Printing is extremely important to me. I spent twelve years printing — six years black and white, six years color. Those were the “dark” ages of my life. I was either in a darkroom, a nightclub, or a photo studio. Sometimes I never saw the light of day. Now everything comes through my studio. I oversee all the prints. I still print my own work.

We have a framer in New York and a framer in Berlin — those are the only two we work with.

What the work says is as important as how it looks. Clarity of meaning is essential — especially in works like Negative Currency, where value, material, and image are inseparable.

You mentioned AI earlier before we started recording. I’d love to go back there for a moment.

I mean, artificial intelligence exists. I don’t know about artificial creativity. AI can pull from other things, but imagination is different. I look at some pictures I’ve made and you’d never know where the influences came from unless I told you.

Take Spaghetti Drama. The top part reminds people of Eggleston’s red room. The bottom comes from Magical Mystery Tour — that scene where the women are stirring a giant pot of spaghetti.

I wasn’t consciously thinking about either of those. Those images were just stored in me from childhood. They come out intuitively.

That feels closer to memory than quotation.

Exactly. And that’s why behind-the-scenes images matter now. People need proof that these things existed in time. If they were illustrations, I wouldn’t be ashamed of that — but they’re not. They existed. They were built. I photographed them.

Let’s come back to Tower of Babel.

It’s about what’s happening right now. Everyone is talking. No one is listening. Everyone has a platform — podcasts, comments, opinions — but there’s no empathy. Even within groups that supposedly agree, people are divided. It feels like we can’t understand each other anymore.

You’ve spoken about education and learning how to think.

I thought college was a place where you heard different opinions and then made up your own mind. I didn’t think it was a place to be indoctrinated. I dropped out of high school at fifteen. I was truant, living and working in New York, but I kept drawing and painting.

I got accepted to the North Carolina School of the Arts based on my drawings. That was a huge break for me. That’s where I learned photography. Photography scared me at first — all those numbers. I was terrible at math.

But I realized how intuitive it was. The lens is like the eye. The darkroom became intuitive. I did wild experiments — painting on negatives, reversing colors. Once I picked up a camera, I never finished another drawing.

You learned collaboration early on.

Working for Andy Warhol at Interview was huge. Andy asked everyone their opinion — interns included.

That stayed with me. I remember asking interns which print they preferred. Sometimes you want a fresh eye — someone without technical training — to tell you what feels right. That openness makes the work better.

Photography is collaborative by nature. Some artists don’t want that, and that’s valid. Someone like Nan Goldin is documenting her life. That’s different. What I do requires many voices.

Climate and spirituality run through a lot of the work.

Climate change has been on my radar for over thirty years — work like Gas and Land SCAPE came directly out of that awareness.

Biblically, after the flood, the promise was that water wouldn’t end the world again. So the opposite would be fire. We’re living like nothing’s wrong, but it feels like a different chapter now. Multiple existential threats at once.

There’s also a turn toward balance.

I went through a very dark period. For Men Will Be Lovers of Self & The Sorrows came from that. I was a workaholic for twenty years. I had rules — I always needed a cover, something in the top ten on TRL, something on VH1. Work was my safe place. Like an addiction.

Eventually I needed balance. I found a place in Maui — an old abandoned nudist colony — and turned it into an off-the-grid farm. I went back to painting on negatives — works like BeHold and Golden Sabine. Some are from the eighties, some are recent. It’s all connected.

This exhibition spans decades. What do you hope people take away?

Not every image needs to be deep. Life has a shallow end and a deep end. Humor, escapism, fashion — they all belong. The celebrity work brings young people into museums. Then they see work that can’t exist on a phone screen. I don’t separate it anymore. It’s all one body of work.

I can’t think of a better note to end on. Thank you so much David.

Thank you. It was a great conversation.

David LaChapelle — Vanishing Act
VISU Contemporary, Miami Beach
29 November 2025 – 31 January 2026

Vanishing Act brings together more than 30 works spanning four decades of David LaChapelle’s career, including the world premiere of nine new pieces. The exhibition traces the evolution of his practice from early pop-cultural spectacle to later works concerned with environmental collapse, spirituality, and the fragility of contemporary belief systems. Large-scale constructed tableaus appear alongside hand-painted negatives and intimate allegorical works, emphasizing LaChapelle’s continued commitment to physical craft and analog image-making in an increasingly simulated visual culture.

Acerca de David LaChapelle

David LaChapelle es un fotógrafo y director americano cuyo trabajo ha desempeñado un papel definitorio en la formación de la cultura visual contemporánea desde finales de los años 80. Después de ser descubierto por Andy Warhol y contratado para trabajar en la revista Interview, LaChapelle rápidamente se hizo conocido por sus fotografías hipersaturadas, teatralmente escenificadas que puenteaban la moda, el retrato de celebridades y el arte fino.

Durante su carrera, su trabajo ha aparecido en importantes publicaciones internacionales y ha sido expuesto en museos y galerías de todo el mundo. Mientras sus primeras imágenes se asociaban con el exceso de pop y la cultura de la celebridad, la práctica de LaChapelle se ha convertido cada vez más en temas de fe, ansiedad ambiental, consumismo y cálculo espiritual. Sus obras posteriores reflejan un interés sostenido en la mitología, la iconografía religiosa y la tensión entre el espectáculo y las creencias.

En cuatro décadas, LaChapelle se ha comprometido a crear conjuntos físicos, pintar negativos y trabajar con artesanos cuyos oficios son cada vez más raros. Su trabajo continúa desafiando las distinciones entre la fotografía comercial y el arte fino, insistiendo en la fotografía como objeto construido y espejo cultural.

Prefacio

Las imágenes de David LaChapelle son inmediatamente reconocibles: saturadas, teatrales, meticulosamente escenificadas y sin duda máximas. A partir de los mundos de las revistas de moda, la cultura pop y la revista de entrevista bajo la mentoría de Andy Warhol, ha pasado décadas colapsando los límites entre la fotografía comercial, el arte fino y el espectáculo.

En los últimos años, estas preocupaciones han llegado a un enfoque más agudo. Las obras ambientales se sientan junto a las alegorías espirituales, los negativos pintados a mano con los manteleros de gran escala, y el humor da paso a la pena, la ansiedad y la reflexión incómoda. En un momento en que la fotografía se aplana cada vez más en pantallas, impulsos y simulaciones, LaChapelle continúa insistiendo en el acto físico de hacer imágenes—construyendo escenas, pintando espacio, pintando fotografías y haciendo imágenes.

Conocí a LaChapelle rodeado de este cuerpo de trabajo, y nuestra conversación se desarrolló menos como una entrevista formal que una meditación sostenida sobre la artesanía, la colaboración, la autoría y la supervivencia. Hablamos de procesos analógicos en una era digital, el trabajo detrás de sus imágenes más ambiciosas, el papel de la colaboración en su estudio, y cómo su relación con el trabajo, la fe y el equilibrio ha cambiado con el tiempo.

Entrevista

Quiero empezar ampliamente. Has vivido varios cambios importantes en la fotografía — cultural, tecnológica, económica. Cuando miras de nuevo cuando empezaste, ¿qué te parece más diferente del mundo cuando entraste en contra del que estás trabajando ahora?

Sí. Mis héroes. Avedon comenzó joven, como yo, trabajando dentro de revistas — Hearst, Condé Nast, publicidad— y murió bajo ese mismo sistema. Eso me importaba cuando era joven, viendo ese camino, viendo que podías vivir toda tu vida dentro de la fotografía.

La fotografía ha cambiado tan dramáticamente desde que empecé a tomar fotos. Primero era analógico. Luego llegó Photoshop. Y luego el Internet realmente, realmente tomó el control. Recuerdo cuando la gente hablaba de lo que estaba en Vanity FairEn realidad, la gente hablaba de ello, había contratos, contratos reales. Rolling Stone, Condé Nast Traveler - había presupuestos, había tiempo, había espacio para hacer cosas.

Ese ecosistema entero ya no existe. Así que estoy agradecido de seguir trabajando, honestamente. Y con todo ese cambio, lo más importante para mí era aprender a evolucionar en lugar de luchar contra él. Pero al mismo tiempo, he tratado muy duro de mantener mi creencia en una visión analógica.

La gente mira el trabajo ahora y asumen que es AI o montado digitalmente, pero no lo es. Solía odiar las imágenes detrás de los escenarios. Realmente las odiaba. Sentí como que regalaron la magia. Pero ahora dispago detrás de las escenas por todo, porque quiero que haya pruebas. Prueba de que estas imágenes fueron construidas, no se armaron más tarde en un ordenador.

Cuando dices "construido", ¿cómo es eso realmente para ti? ¿Por qué importa que la gente entienda ese proceso?

Porque creo en lo que hago. Realmente lo hago. Y el trabajo es teatral — toma mucha habilidad de mucha gente. Constructores. Pintores. Proyectores. Diseñadores. Iluminación de la gente. Todo.

Tomar todo ese trabajo y colapsar en un autor digital no es justo. El crédito pertenece a la gente que realmente construyó estas cosas. La Torre de Babel todavía se sienta en mi estudio. Es físicamente allí. El cielo está arrasado — eso es un arte moribundo. He trabajado con tal vez tres artistas de aerógrafos en toda mi carrera. Simplemente no lo encuentras más.

Esos fondos —la pintura de los aerógrafos, la iluminación— son verdaderos oficios. En los años setenta había un montón de artistas de aerógrafos. Ahora ya casi se ha ido. Así que cuando alguien dice, "Oh, eso es sólo digital", borra a la gente que lo hizo.

Esos fondos —la pintura de los aerógrafos, la iluminación— son artesanías que están desapareciendo. Para llamar que un composite digital borra el trabajo de las personas que lo hicieron.

La colaboración se siente inseparable de cómo trabajas.

Completamente. Quiero ver que los mesetas existen delante de mí. No soy un tipo de ordenador. Quiero ver los conjuntos, los trajes, la iluminación, el casting, todo.

Hay una adrenalina precipitada a eso. Es teatral. La noche de apertura es el rodaje. Los flashes se apagan. Eché un montón de bailarines porque son muy libres con sus cuerpos. Cuando hemos terminado, la gente anima. Realmente se siente como una actuación.

Sueño con estar en sets todo el tiempo. O estoy en una sesión de fotos, o estoy cazando apartamento en Nueva York. Esos son mis dos sueños recurrentes.

Los apartamentos de Nueva York eran extáticos y traumáticos al mismo tiempo. Conseguí mi primer escuadrón cuando tenía dieciséis años, en la tercera calle entre la avenida A y B en 1979. Luego, lo sublevé a un amigo que me lo mantuvo. La gente era despiadado sobre los apartamentos.

Todavía tengo sueños sobre eso, y sobre estar en juego.

¿Todavía llevas esa energía una vez que la imagen está terminada?

Soy adicto a esa sensación durante el rodaje. Completamente adicto. Pero una vez que está hecho, no pienso realmente en el proceso más a menos que lo estoy explicando. Luego se vuelve sobre la composición. Sobre la impresión.

La impresión es muy importante para mí. Pasé doce años imprimiendo — seis años blanco y negro, seis años de color. Ésas eran las edades de mi vida “o oscuras”. Yo estaba en un cuarto oscuro, un club nocturno, o un estudio de fotos. A veces nunca vi la luz del día. Ahora todo viene a través de mi estudio. Yo superviso todas las impresiones. Todavía imprimí mi propio trabajo.

Tenemos una fotogramadora en Nueva York y una fotogramadora en Berlín, son los únicos dos con los que trabajamos.

Lo que dice el trabajo es tan importante como lo parece. La claridad del significado es esencial, especialmente en obras como Moneda negativa, donde el valor, el material y la imagen son inseparables.

Mencionaste a AI antes de empezar a grabar. Me encantaría volver allí por un momento.

Quiero decir, la inteligencia artificial existe. No sé sobre la creatividad artificial. AI puede sacar de otras cosas, pero la imaginación es diferente. Miro algunas fotos que he hecho y nunca sabrías de dónde vienen las influencias a menos que te lo haya dicho.

Toma. Spaghetti Drama. La parte superior recuerda a la gente de la sala roja de Eggleston. La parte inferior viene de Magical Mystery Tour - esa escena donde las mujeres están revolviendo una olla gigante de espaguetis.

No estaba pensando conscientemente en ninguno de esos. Esas imágenes sólo se almacenaban en mí desde la infancia. Ellos salen intuitivamente.

Eso se siente más cerca de la memoria que la cita.

Exactamente. Y por eso las imágenes detrás de escena importan ahora. La gente necesita pruebas de que estas cosas existieron en el tiempo. Si fueran ilustraciones, no me avergonzaría de eso, pero no lo son. Ellos existieron. Fueron construidos. Yo las fotografié.

Volvamos a Torre de Babel.

Se trata de lo que está sucediendo ahora mismo. Todo el mundo está hablando. Nadie está escuchando. Todo el mundo tiene una plataforma — podcasts, comentarios, opiniones — pero no hay empatía. Incluso dentro de grupos que supuestamente están de acuerdo, la gente está dividida. Se siente como que no podemos entendernos más.

Habéis hablado de educación y de aprender a pensar.

Pensé que la universidad era un lugar donde escuchaste opiniones diferentes y luego te inventaste la mente. No pensé que era un lugar para ser adoctrinado. Salí de la escuela secundaria a los quince años. Yo era fiel, vivía y trabajaba en Nueva York, pero yo seguía dibujando y pintando.

Me aceptaron a la Escuela de Artes de Carolina del Norte basándose en mis dibujos. Eso fue un gran descanso para mí. Ahí es donde aprendí la fotografía. La fotografía me asustó al principio — todos esos números. Yo era terrible en matemáticas.

Pero me di cuenta de lo intuitivo que era. La lente es como el ojo. El cuarto oscuro se hizo intuitivo. Hice experimentos salvajes — pintando en negativos, revirtiendo colores. Una vez que recogí una cámara, nunca terminé otro dibujo.

Aprendiste la colaboración temprano.

Trabajando para Andy Warhol en Entrevista Andy preguntó a todos su opinión —entrenadores incluidos.

Recuerdo haber preguntado a los internos que imprimen que preferían. A veces quieres un ojo fresco —alguien sin entrenamiento técnico— para decirte lo que se siente bien. Esa apertura hace que el trabajo sea mejor.

La fotografía es colaborativa por la naturaleza. Algunos artistas no quieren eso, y eso es válido. Alguien como Nan Goldin está documentando su vida. Eso es diferente. Lo que hago requiere muchas voces.

El clima y la espiritualidad corren a través de una gran cantidad de trabajo.

El cambio climático ha estado en mi radar desde hace más de treinta años, trabajo como Gas and Land SCAPE Salió directamente de esa conciencia.

Bíblicamente, después de la inundación, la promesa era que el agua no terminaría el mundo de nuevo. Así que lo contrario sería fuego. Vivimos como nada está mal, pero se siente como un capítulo diferente ahora. Múltiples amenazas existenciales a la vez.

También hay un giro hacia el equilibrio.

Pasé por un período muy oscuro. Para los hombres serán amantes del Ser " Las penas Yo era un adicto al trabajo durante veinte años. Tenía reglas — siempre necesitaba una cubierta, algo en los diez primeros en la TRL, algo en la VH1. El trabajo era mi lugar seguro. Como una adicción.

Eventualmente necesitaba equilibrio. Encontré un lugar en Maui —una antigua colonia nudista abandonada— y la convertí en una granja fuera de la granja. Volví a pintar en negativos — obras como BeHold y Golden Sabine. Algunos son de los años ochenta, algunos son recientes. Está todo conectado.

Esta exposición abarca décadas. ¿Qué esperas que la gente se lleve?

No toda imagen tiene que ser profunda. La vida tiene un extremo poco profundo y un fondo profundo. Humor, escapismo, moda — todos pertenecen. El trabajo de la celebridad trae a los jóvenes a los museos. Luego ven trabajo que no puede existir en una pantalla de teléfono. Ya no la separa. Es todo un cuerpo de trabajo.

No puedo pensar en una mejor nota para terminar. Muchas gracias David.

Fue una gran conversación.

About Maren Levinson

Maren Levinson is the founder of REDEYE, an artist’s agency, based in Los Angeles, representing a diverse pool of artists all over the United States.

Before starting Redeye, Maren was a photo editor at Mother Jones Magazine, and the founding photo editor at Dwell Magazine. Foreword

Careers don’t always start with ambition. Sometimes they start with attention—with noticing who made the picture, not just what’s in it.

In this conversation, we sit down with the founder of Redeye, whose career has been built on recognizing voice and standing beside it, rather than stepping in front of it. This is a story about collaboration, about knowing when your role is to listen, to advocate, and to create space for other people’s work to exist in the world.

The interview moves quickly from origin to reckoning. What once felt like a durable creative industry now feels unsettled—budgets thinner, volume gone, technology accelerating faster than taste can keep up. AI looms not as theory, but as pressure.

There are no predictions here. Just clarity. About responsibility. About authorship. About what still matters when certainty disappears.

Read this as a temperature check. Not for where photography was—but for where it might still go.

-Agustin Sanchez, Publisher
